speechtext: 127. Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries, including $25,900 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the governor in council, $193,711.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I am glad that this item gives the committee an opportunity to consider again the question of penal reform. I know that this subject is not a new one, and that it is considered annually, usually on this item in the estimates of the Minister of Justice. But no member of this committee need offer apologies for again raising his voice on the imperative necessity of giving due attention to the subject of penal reform in Canada.
One of the most hopeful things that has happened since last year's debate was the enlargement of the commission last August. The committee will recall that General Gibson, chief commissioner of penitentiaries, was appointed some two and a half years ago. On August 20 last the Minister of Justice-announced the appointment of two deputy commissioners: Mr. Joseph McCulley, who for some years had been headmaster of Pickering Boys College and a leader in boys'

__________ Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
educational work in Canada, and Dr. Louis Philippe Gendreau, the chief psychiatrist at the Manitoba Mental Hospital.
When this item was under debate in the house on June 27, 1946, I uttered1 words of strong approval of the appointment of General Gibson as chief commissioner. I should like now to commend' the appointment of the two deputy commissioners. It has been my good fortune to know Mr. McCulley personally for some years. We have had common interests in some aspects of boys' work. I regard his appointment as a most suitable one, for which the Minister of Justice should be highly commended. It is not my privilege to know Doctor Gendreau, personally, but from what I have heard about him I believe his appointment also was a most suitable one.
With a strong commission made up of these three eminent men, I think the public will have been led by this time to expect action in the field of penal reform. I urge upon the minister that he give to these three commissioners ample opportunity and a reasonably free hand to assume the task of penal reform. I hope he will give them every encouragement to take the Archambault report of 1938 and endeavour to make its recommendations a reality. Ten years have passed since this monumental report was written, with its eighty-eight recommendations, some of which have been carried into effect, but many of which have not. I conceive it to be the duty of parliament to continue to apply pressure to see that these salutary recommendations receive adequate consideration, and that they are given effect just as soon as possible.
In my humble opinion it would be a useful thing if we had a committee of this house which could1 hear the commissioners at first hand, receive a report of such progress as they have been able to make in the matter of penal reform, and discuss with them their plans for the future. There are grave limitations upon going into a matter of this kind in adequate detail in committee of the whole. We can address our remarks to the Chair and the minister can make his observations, but we do not have an opportunity of questioning the commissioners, who are dealing with the problem personally; or of discussing with them their plans for approaching the problem of reform. I am convinced that if this commission is given an opportunity, we shall see definite progress made in the direction of penal reform. At the same time I am conscious, as I think are all the members of the committee, of the need which still exists for it.
I am sure the committee is well acquainted with the unhappy results of several recent escapes from the penitentiary. I should like to mention two of them. One of them resulted in homicide, and one of the two persons who escaped was one of the four boys who had been involved in the homicide of a resident of my own constituency; the famous Tobias case. Speaking in this house on June 27, 1946, on the question of penal reform. I undertook to make some remarks upon that case-of course after it had been concluded. It happens that at that time those young men had been convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to penal terms by Mr. Justice Keiller Mackay, the trial judge. One of these young men was involved in the recent jail break which resulted in the death of the prison guard at Kingston. It emphasizes the necessity of seeing that juries really do their duty as such; that they be not swept away by maudlin sentiment, and points to the results that flow from the failure of juries, to carry out their duty under the law.
There was another unfortunate jail break in September of last year which resulted in the escape of three notorious criminals, Mickey Macdonald, Ulysses Lauzon and Nick Minnille. The chief commissioner, General Gibson, issued a statement following that escape, in which he indicated that an intensive investigation had been made and that administrative changes had been effected with a view to promoting efficiency of administration in the penitentiary. No system can be perfect, but I think that matters of this kind could usefully engage the attention of a committee of this house.
There is another side to the matter of penitentiary administration which I think warrants consideration by the committee. I wish to refer to a statement made by the chief coroner for Ontario, Doctor Smirle Lawson, following an investigation which he carried out in August of last year. It may be, Mr. Chairman, that the matter referred to in this statement by Doctor Lawson has been investigated by the commissioners, and that the situation disclosed in this statement has been remedied and redress made. But I have seen no public statement in regard to it, and I bring it before the committee of the whole because I think it is a matter that should receive its attention.
In the Globe and Mail of August 7,. 1947, we have this article under the heading "Charges T.B. convicts not segregated at pen." The article reads in part as follows:
Convicts with tuberculosis in its advanced stages are kept in close contact with non-
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

tuberculosis patients in the Kingston penitentiary infirmary, chief coroner Smirle Lawson charged last night.	_
The chief coroner declared the prison hospital was overcrowded and its equipment inadequate, particularly in the operating room. He made these observations on the basis of an official visit to the prison after a convict, Carl Woverenvitz, 57. had died1 in Christie street hospital.
Following Doctor Lawson's remarks, a coroner's jury investigating the death of Woverenvitz demanded that the federal government take immediate steps to segregate tuberculous and non-tuberculous convicts in the penitentiary hospital.
AVoverenvitz did not have tuberculosis but died of complications arising from a wound he received during the first great war. He was treated in the penitentiary hospital and in Kingston general hospital before being moved to Christie street. The inquest was held because the law requires that a public inquiry be held whenever a convict dies while serving his sentence.
Doctor Lawson declared the prison infirmary was well run and spotlessly clean. He also praised the surgeon in charge, Doctor Thomas Tweddell. But Doctor Tweddell, he Baid, could do little in the face of the hospital conditions.
"I found that where Woverenvitz had been lying in the prison hospital there were advanced cases of pulmonary tuberculosis which other patients might quite easily contract," Dr. Lawson said. He added that the infirmary was small and that the proximity of tuberculosis and other patients was "not good medical practice."
Dr. I. H. Erb, provincial pathologist, was a witness at the inquest. "Would you say," Dr. Lawson asked him "that these tuberculosis cases, under the conditions I have described, were a menace."
"Yes," Dr. Erb agreed. "From your report, I think they would be a menace provided they were in relatively close proximity. They would be especially dangerous to younger men who might not discover their own condition until many years later."	.
Dr. Lawson commented that because men had lost their freedom, that was no reason why they should not get as good medical treatment as patients got in other hospitals.
The jury found that Woverenvitz had received correct treatment from the prison surgeon and at Kingston General and Christie Street hospitals.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the situation here referred to has been remedied. With the kind of men we have on the penitentiaries commission I would expect that, on this very serious matter being brought to their attention, they would have acted promptly to remedy it; but I think it should engage the attention of the house, and I hope the minister will be able to make some statement with regard to it.
From many sides we are hearing criticism of present conditions. We hear the youth of today castigated, and we hear different panaceas put forward as solutions for the problem of crime among youth. As one who has sought to interest himself in youth and its problems

I want to express my profound disagreement with some of those who are busy denouncing the youth of today. I see the superintendent of one reformatory has said:
Never at any time in the past twenty-five years has youth been found so insolent, so defiant, or so determined1 to do what is wrong as at the present time.
I think those words are unduly harsh. Those of us who have tried to keep in close touch with the youth of our respective communities will believe the youth of today are as good as were the youth of any other generation. On the other hand, however, they live in a very different kind of world, a fact which the older generation does not always take into account. Life is far more complicated; but fundamentally at the root of the problems of crime and delinquency among youth today is the question of control of children by their parents. It is not so much the failure of the youth of today, or delinquency on the part of the youth of today, as it is the failure on the part of the parents and the home. Everything that is weakening the influence of the home and weakening parental control and a sense of parental responsibility for youth is a detriment to our community. One of our great problems is the insidious pressure of materialistic forces and materialistic philosophies, striving to defeat religious and moral teaching which has its heart and centre in the home and the church. Anything we as men in public life can do to support healthy community influences, which in turn will not supplant but will help strengthen a healthy home influence, I am sure we will all consider it our duty to do.
There is one other aspect of this problem of which we should never lose sight, and that is the problem of the discharged prisoner. Much can be done in the early stages, of course, to guide the footsteps of youth into the paths of good citizenship and useful life. When youth goes astray, much can be done to guide its footsteps back into paths that will lead to useful life in the community. But there is a third aspect, a third stage of the problem, which at all times must engage our interest and concern. That is the problem of the discharged prisoner, the man who has gone astray, who has served a term and is released from a penal institution, only to be confronted by a world which may look to him quite different from the world he left when he was convicted; a world which in so many cases seems cold, unfriendly and inhospitable to him. Each of us, I am sure, has had experience with cases of this kind, but I wish to mention one which arose in an Ontario court some months ago. It is an example of the way in which a prison record dogs a man even when he is trying to

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaiies
go straight. It is an illustration of the fact that discharged prisoners, after they have paid their debt to society, need assistance from various quarters, not only from institutions such as the John Howard society, which is doing magnificent work, but from all who regard themselves as good citizens.
This was a case that came before the county court judge in Windsor. The man in question, whose name I shall not mention, was charged with uttering a forged cheque. The prisoner, who was just twenty-five years of age, had something to say when the court was about to pass sentence upon him. He referred to his police record as a nemesis and said that he believed society had failed in its treatment of men released from prison. He had been convicted first when a third-year university student. One would have thought he was in a position to advance himself into a career of usefulness to society, but he was convicted while attending university. Later he enlisted in the R.C.A.F.; but when his prison record became known he was discharged, just as he was about to receive a commission. That record, with one blot added to another, prevented him from obtaining a bond in one civilian position which otherwise would have been available to him, and it led to his discharge from a position in a Toronto munitions plant. This is what the prisoner himself had to say in court, as the judge was about to pass a further sentence upon him:
My understanding is that society, through the legislature, enacts laws for its own protection. But when a man comes out that debt is paid, and if society hinders or hampers him in his return to them, then society has failed.
The crown attorney commented, "There is something in what he says."
I am not one of those who take a superficial or unnecessarily sentimental view of our treatment of those who have gone wrong. I do not believe we should approach this question in terms of mere sloppy sentiment. I do think, however, that a great deal remains to be done. It is not a task we can simply leave to such beneficent institutions and organizations as the John Howard society, to which I have referred already, which are doing so much to help to rehabilitate discharged prisoners. We cannot rely simply upon individuals. In that regard I should like to pay tribute to the outstanding work done by the former chief of police in Toronto, General D. C. Draper, who is president of the John Howard society, and who did so much in the formation of the Prisoners' Rehabilitation Society which, several years ago, became the John Howard society. But it is incumbent upon all of us who regard 5849-314
ourselves as servants of the public to do all we can to arouse the public to a sense of its responsibilities to these men. Given a fair opportunity, given guidance and friendly help when they come out, the great majority of them will go straight, as one can prove by statistics. But given a hostile or unfriendly reception, and being denied employment and the opportunity to find a place in and be useful to society, then we are simply inviting them to tread again the path of crime.
I am proud of Ontario and the commendable lead taken in that province in the setting up of a department of reform institutions under a minister whose task it is to seek as soon as possible to carry out extensive reforms in the penal institutions of that province, to see that youthful offenders are not permitted to mingle with hardened criminals, that different types of criminals are segregated, and that the guiding principle behind all our prison administration shall be the reform and training in useful pursuits of those who are incarcerated, so that they may upon discharge find a place in society. The purpose is that they may regard themselves as useful members of society, and not as enemies of society. This, of course, cannot be done overnight, but it is a commendable lead and one which could be widely followed.
I hope what I have said today has been constructive. I repeat what I said at the outset, that I commend the Minister of Justice for the two appointments made last year to the penitentiaries commission. They were such as to lead many of us to be hopeful that substantial reforms will be made in those penal institutions which are under the jurisdiction of the dominion.
Again I urge upon the minister to encourage the commission to take in hand the responsibility for carrying forward the task of reform and implementation of the recommendations of the Archambault report, and the modernization of our penal system.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, coming from a constituency which has within its boundaries a large penitentiary, I have an interest in the people employed there and, like the hon. member who preceded me, I am interested in the people who are confined there.
I should like to draw the matter of wages to the minister's attention. The cost of living has gone up by 153 points. The wages of those employed in prisons have not increased by anything like that amount. The Archambault report emphasizes particularly the fact that persons employed in prisons were not at that time being paid wages as high as were paid to those who cleaned the streets of our cities.
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

I made that statement before, and upon checking it again I find it still to be true.
I find this at page 344 of the Archambault report:
Your commissioners are convinced that the success or failure of the recommendations contained in this report will depend almost entirely upon the prison personnel to be charged with carrying out the recommendations. The success of every prison system is dependent upon the type of officers in that system.
On the next page of the report the commission says, commenting on some surveys it had made:
No matter what public service one deals 'with -social or fighting-if the personnel is not the right type for t'he work in question-I stress that, for the work in question-the results will be poor. This is particularly so in service where the main preoccupation of the staff is in dealing with human beings as opposed to finance or commerce. In no public social service is this more true than in the prison world where we have to deal with both sexes; men and women of all strata of society, old and young in years of crime, rich and poor, the good and the bad, and, in some cases, the very bad.
I am sure the minister will realize that if we do not pay proper wages it will be hopeless to get the type of men we need for these prisons. The hours they work should compare favourably with those worked by ordinary tradesmen, but in fact they work much longer hours.
By order in council 33/2047 an increase of $5 a month is given to guard grade I, guard messenger, and guard storeman. Let me point out that an advance of $5 in these times is not enough, in view of the present cost of living. I say they are entitled to much better wages than that.
The prison authorities have come to realize that they do not want men like the old sergeant-majors under whom I have served. Those old imperial sergeant-majors set out first to break your heart, even if they accomplished nothing else. That was the type of man who was employed in prisons in earlier days.
I have served under such men. But in the modem world they are not accepted as fit for work in our prisons. Prison discipline and the management of our prisoners have made great progress in recent years. If we want the right men, we will have to pay wages equal to those received by men doing similar work in other spheres.
I shall not at this time go into the question of superannuation. I still have not had satisfaction in connection with the complaint I made last year that a man who has paid his debt to the government under a superannuation scheme, who has paid everything he owed with compound interest, should have to keep on paying until the day he dies.

There is another thing I want to bring up- the housing at Stony Mountain. For three or four years now I have appealed to the government to do something. Here is what the Archambault report has to say about housing:
The accommodation for the staff is inadequate. It is unreasonable and unnecessarily humiliating to ask the members of the staff to live under the conditions that now exist in the officers' tenements 'belonging to the institution. These houses were built fifty years ago; they are without sanitary conveniences, and prisoners themselves are much more comfortably housed in their cells than the officers in the penitentiary tenements.
Your commissioners are of the opinion that this state of affairs is destructive of the morale of the officers and that immediate steps should be taken to provide the staff and their families with respectable accommodation. In a large metropolitan centre the homes which are provided for the staff would, indeed, be condemned by the medical .authorities.
Even with the scarcity of building materials, the Department of Justice should be able to do something. Bowling alleys and picture shows are still being built; surely the government can get some lumber and start some houses here. The greatest objection is that there are no sanitary conveniences.
Like the hon. gentleman who preceded me, I have always been interested in the care of the young criminal or first offender. It is unfortunate that more progress cannot be made in establishing the Borstal system or some equivalent system to care for our first offenders. Our penitentiaries today are for punishment more than for corrective purposes or the reform of the convict. Our system has a tendency to make an habitual criminal out of the first offender. He is put in with hardened criminals or men who have been convicted many times. Under the present system it is practically impossible to segregate the hardened criminal from the first offender. Someone sent me a copy of "Must Canada Continue to Create Criminals?" and I should like to quote from the second page as follows:
The Borstal system of schools in England, for the reclamation of lads who are considered to have a chance, has proved its value. To be a success here, however, as they have been in England, the whole English system must be adopted. The juvenile court there, dealing with children from seven to fifteen, is the handmaiden of the Borstal system, which deals with lads from 16 to 23. The two reforms must go hand in hand.
In the report of the commissioner dated February 5, 1947, the following appears on page 15:
The royal commission dealt at length with the methods of treatment of young offenders between the ages of 16 and 21 and recommended the adoption in Canada of the principles of the Borstal system which has been developed in the United Kingdom. Your commissioner is con-

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
vinced that the principles of that system offer the best known opportunity for the reformation and rehabilitation of youths who have not yet become hardened criminals, and considers that any new institutions to be established by the government of Canada should be of a type to permit the adoption of those principles thereby enabling youths of the reformable type to be withdrawn from the penitentiaries for adults. It cannot be too strongly emphasized, however, that the success of the Borstal system depends primarly on the trained personnel it attracts to its service. It has been said that the foundations of the Borstal system are first the recruitment of the right men, then their proper training, and finally their full co-operation with one another in an atmosphere of freedom and mutual understanding.
I commend the reading of that to hon. members because it shows what can be done. But it must be remembered that wages will have to be increased in order to make this service attractive to people who can do a good job. The scheme advocated in the commissioner's report would be a step in the right direction. A system of this kind would tend to improve the effectiveness of our penal institutions, but no adequate system can be adopted until the indiscriminate herding of criminals in penal institutions is abolished. No doubt some wardens have attempted to discriminate between different offenders, but segregation under one roof cannot be very effective. Different classes of prisons will have to be set apart for young convicts who should receive Borstal treatment. Another prison could be set aside for first offenders and those who may be reclaimed for a law-abiding life. And of course there should be separate institutions for the habitual criminal who is a menace to society.
I do not want to take up any more time, because I think the minister knows what I am driving at. I want better wages for those who are going to try to correct these people. It does not matter how bad a man is; there is some good in him, and we should have some system that would try to bring out that good.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not discuss the Borstal system, because I did that on two previous occasions after making extensive surveys of the system as carried out in the prisons in England. What I want to bring particularly to the attention of the minister today is what can be done to reclaim prisoners. Frequently our talk is about prison reform but I have spent much of my time on methods of reclaiming prisoners. A previous speaker said that the prisoner should be taken care of after he gets out of the penitentiary. I have found that one of the main causes of a released prisoner again lapsing 5849-314J
into crime is his inability to get a job, as the previous speaker mentioned, or a lack of funds.
I have been able to get jobs for many released prisoners, but I tell the minister it is quite a task. I have had to call up manufacturers and heads of firms and give my own personal undertaking that the prisoner would do a decent job. I am happy to say that in every case in which I have done that, the released prisoner has lived up to my best expectations. I try to treat them as a father would, and direct them in the right way. In their minds perhaps the best way to direct them in the right way is to get them jobs.
I should like to know what is being done by the department for prisoners after they are released. Let me refer to a tragic case that came up in Toronto recently. It was that of a well-known convict by the name of Hopkins. Here is his record as published in the Toronto Evening Telegram, after he had been shot to death recently by a constable while engaged in robbing a store:
1930. Convicted of theft at Hamilton; suspended sentence.
1932. Convicted of housebreaking, theft and breaking of recognizance; sent to the Victoria industrial school for an indefinite period.
1934.	Convicted of breach of recognizance; given four months definite and eight months indefinite.
1934.	Convicted again at St. Catharines of breaking and entering; given four months in jail.
1935.	Convicted of theft; given six months definite and nine months indefinite.
1936.	Convicted of carrying an unlawful weapon and being in possession of an unregistered revolver; given three months in jail on the first count and fined $50 or 30 days on the second.
1937.	Convicted on August 1 of shopbreaking and theft; given five years in Kingston.
1941. Convicted of shopbreaking and theft and possession of loaded revolver; given five years on first charge and two years on second, to run consecutively.
1947. Convicted on December 12 on a charge of receiving; given one year.
Within the last month or six weeks he was caught with another convict breaking into a store and was shot dead in the lane behind the store. It is a tragic story-ten arrests and ten convictions within a comparatively few years. What is being done to reform or reclaim prisoners, if they can be reclaimed? I am convinced that the department and whoever is helping the department outside should make a
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

much stronger effort to reclaim prisoners. This man Hopkins, after ten arrests and ten convictions in little more than a ten-year period, ended up by being shot. There are many cases of the kind, but I shall not take the time to give more examples. Is there any branch of the department that is making a strenuous effort to reclaim prisoners, if they can be reclaimed? Of course the Borstal system will help a great deal, but when a convict cannot be reclaimed, as apparently was the case with Hopkins, should he not be declared incorrigible and be put away for good? Every day we read of criminals who, after serving a term in a penitentiary, were released and committed a murder or some other crime much worse than the one they were sent down for.
I would say that the department should do one of two things: either reclaim these convicts or put them away for good. It has been said, and I agree, that the home has the greatest influence of all, and the sooner homes get back to the old habit of family worship, under which I was raised, the better it will be for the children. I can see my parents yet, reading a chapter out of the scriptures every morning, and then, after explaining it to us, offering up a prayer. There is not so much of that done in these days as there should be.
I recognize the tremendous job which the department and the police have to do. Nevertheless one of two things should be done: either the convict should be reclaimed, or when it is found he cannot be reclaimed, he should be put away for good.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I believe that a real work of reform is being done in some of our penal institutions. I refer particularly to Saskatchewan penitentiary, where the work done in the past few years has been such as to result in a minimum of recidivists. I know of several cases I could bring to the attention of the committee, but I do not propose to do so. I think it is only fair to say that while in certain areas recidivism is of serious proportions, the work being done in Saskatchewan penitentiary has been highly commendable. I know of one man who, after serving a long period in that penitentiary fol-owing his conviction for murder, was allowed out on parole some four years ago, joined the army, rose to the rank of sergeant, and is now back in the area in which he lived prior to commission of the crime, and is taking his place in society in a manner commendable both to him and to the system operated in the penitentiary of Saskatchewan. That young man entered the penitentiary at the age of eighteen or nineteen with a grade 2 education, and at the end of fourteen years he was

discharged from that institution with the equivalent of grade 12 education.
The new commissioner of penitentiaries has an important and responsible position, and one that is difficult by reason of two forces sometimes pulling in opposite directions- punishment for wrongdoing, and reform. One worthy thing that has been done during the past year is the establishment of a policy of education and training for penitentiary officers. Some twenty-five of them have taken the course. To be a successful penitentiary officer requires not only the capacity to appreciate human shortcomings and the ability to enforce discipline, but also the capacity for intelligent coercion. The hon. member for Selkirk referred to the old type of officer who was an autocrat and sometimes a martinet. That type of officer is rapidly leaving the penitentiary service of this country, and properly so. But you cannot get the type of officers who are needed in the penitentiaries at the present rates of pay. A penitentiary officer receives a low salary having regard to present living costs-it runs from $125 to $140 or $150 a month-and he has no security. He is a temporary official who can be removed at any time. His right to be made permanent was done away with some fifteen years ago. It is a serious situation. It was done that way because it was thought that those in charge of the various institutions would not be able to exercise proper discipline if there were permanence in the appointments.
I come now to a question that was raised by the hon. member for Eglinton in what I thought was an excellent statement of the problem of penal reform. During the last year-and he made reference to it-there have been a number of penitentiary outbreaks. The minister should indicate to the committee the various penitentiaries in which these outbreaks took place. There have been rumours as to the circumstances under which revolvers and firearms get to the possession of convicts in these institutions. We had an example in Kingston penitentiary of wyhat happens where there is no proper discipline. That is the most recent occurrence. Where did these convicts get possession of the firearms which they used in committing homicide in their escape? In what other penitentiaries in connection with which investigations have taken place in the last year have firearms been found in possession of prisoners? I cannot understand how firearms could get into the possession of convicts without assistance from within. If a lawyer goes to consult his client in the penitentiary he has no opportunity of being in a room with the prisoner. He is placed in the

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
same position as a visitor; he is removed from the prisoner and separated by a net. How do these things occur? What happened? Was anything done to punish wrongdoers within the penitentiary and prevent a recurrence of such incidents?
I should like to say a word in respect to remission of sentences. The present system of remission of sentences is haphazard and uncertain, and in many cases works unfairness among prisoners who are serving terms for similar crimes and offences. Too often the exercise of remissions results from representations which are made, and not from consideration from time to time, by those in authority, of the remainder of the sentence. I mention one case in particular. It is difficult to maintain authority within a penal institution when certain prisoners have their sentences remitted at the end of the minimum period of sentence, and others who have equally conformed to the regulations, find that for some reason nothing is done. I find it difficult to see any rhyme or reason for the granting of remissions. Certainly the principle upon which they should be based, as I see it, is, first, that the sentence served has paid the debt to society; second, that the sentence served has been sufficient to punish the wrongdoer while giving him an opportunity to reform.
I know of a man in the Saskatchewan penitentiary who was sentenced for murder in 1929. If ever there was doubt as to the guilt of a man, there was doubt in that case. I am not going to give his name, but I shall send it to the minister. He was sentenced to death. He had no funds or friends. A certain lawyer, reading of the case in the paper, and believing that that man was entitled to appeal, undertook the appeal, which came before the court of appeal of Saskatchewan. The court dismissed the appeal, but expressed serious doubts with regard to the case. Commutation was granted. My doubts of that case are no less strong today than they were in 1929. That man sees others going out year after year. When an application for remission is made- and his record is perfect; he has discharged any debt to society, if he was guilty, of which there is still doubt, and he continues to protest his innocence-the reason given why he cannot have his remission is that nobody will assume responsibility for him and assure him a livelihood if he were discharged. That seems difficult to understand. There is no doubt about it. The question has been asked over and over again whether anybody will accept responsibility for him. I feel that that is the type of case which the remission branch should
reconsider. The man's record in the penitentiary over nineteen years has been satisfactory. Remissions should be based on the record of the offender. In a case such as the one I have cited there should be no denial of opportunity for a man to take his place in society, even though the difficulties are almost overwhelming, having regard to the period in which he has been a ward of the state.
Mention was made of the John Howard society. Too often do we base success in life on material considerations. I am thinking at the moment of Mr. J. A. Edmison, K.C., a man who has taken over the position, as his life work, of secretary of this society. He sacrifices his profession and his monetary opportunities. During the past two years he has gone across this country, and I think more than anyone else has brought to the attention of the public as a whole the necessity of implementation of many of the recommendations in the Archam-bault report which, for all too long a time, did not receive from the Department of Justice the attention they deserve.
I do not know what can be done to rehabilitate the man who has served his sentence. It is trite to say that he finds grave difficulties. Everyone who practises the law has been told at first hand of men who, after having paid their debt to society, cannot secure employment because of their record. The John Howard society is doing something in that direction to assure assistance in rehabilitation to those men who made a mistake in life, and who have discharged their debt to society. While today some assistance is given to the John Howard society, I hope that I shall not be criticized for advocating a reduction of taxation on the one hand and then asking for additional expenditures on the other, when I ask for consideration by the government to making to that society a grant in order to enable it to expand its activities in this country for the benefit and rehabilitation of those who, having erred, now ask the opportunity to take their place in society.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister if he is in favour of cutting down the sentence of the criminal who has everything in his favour to indicate that he will make good, if somebody will sponsor him. I have had a good deal of experience with these cases. I think I have had about 134 men out under supervision in the past forty years, and only three have failed. The former minister of justice was willing; he thought it was a good thing if a man's sentence was cut down before he served a complete term.
My plan has always been to check up with the chief of police and not to ask for a man
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

to be allowed out unless I interviewed him personally and found out his attitude. When a man is placed on his honour, but when he also knows there is somebody watching him with a live interest in his welfare, week in and week out, it gives him an opportunity to make good.
Only a little while ago I was asked to go out and see if it was possible to get a boy out of the penitentiary. When I went into the home the mother was smoking a cigarette and on the table was a bottle of Canadian rye with the cork out of it. I checked up with the police right away. I said, "Do not touch him. You will get into trouble. He has a bad habit, and he got it from his father and mother." I know some men like to take a drink. But when a boy is taught to drink in his home, he acquires a terribly bad start. But only three- and that is less than three per cent-of those we have had out, have failed. Thanks to the wholehearted co-operation of my better half, those boys were welcomed in our home and they enjoyed the friendship they found there. Does the minister think it is a good thing to have a man out on permit under certain conditions, or does he not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I have just two questions I should like to ask the Minister of Justice; but, before doing so, may I make one comment regarding statements that have been made here this afternoon? It is true that the segregation of criminals has created considerable interest in this country, and the Borstal system has been mentioned by many speakers on many occasions. But I took note that a commission was appointed not so long ago in Great Britain to investigate the Borstal system there; because, under the changed conditions under which we are now living, it appears that conditions have also changed with youth and with adults as well. I know the statement is commonly made that youth should be segregated in penitentiaries from the hardened criminals. But as one who periodically visits the penitentiary in Westminster, I may say I have found that many old hardened criminals have expressed to me the request that they be segregated from some of the present youth who come into the pen. I do not say that in any spirit of levity, or in the way of carping criticism. That is the actual fact. In view of the fact that Great Britain, with its great Borstal system, has found that something has gone wrong with the youth, I am wondering if the minister has any information regarding the commission and what they found out there. I thought I would rise in my place and tell what I had found out in my visits to the penitentiary.

On January 19, in a speech here, I drew the minister's attention to serious complaints with regard to their wages made by guards in the penitentiary at New Westminster. Like the hon. member for Selkirk, I believe these men are doing a special kind of work. If you want to keep them content, it is my opinion that you should at least pay them as much as guards are getting in the provincial prison. Each and everyone of us judges by comparisons. We are all satisfied until we find that somebody else is getting a little more than we are. The guards are human too. The class of work they are doing today has been elevated. We are looking for a higher type of guard to look after the welfare of the men in the penitentiary. I could never understand why guards who look after prisoners in a provincial prison should receive far more than do guards who look after prisoners in the penitentiary, although they may later be looking after the same prisoners that are being looked after in the provincial jail. Has any investigation been made into the request I made on January 19, regarding the salaries and wages paid to these guards?

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I am desirous of commending those who are responsible for the appointment of Joseph McCulley. I say to the Minister of Justice that, from my own personal knowledge, this appointment is one which receives the support of my native province. It so happens that Pickering college, of which he was headmaster, was my alma mater. I have taken a keen interest in that particular institution and have personally observed the work of Joseph McCulley, which had to do with boys in the college where the surroundings were quite different from those he will find in the task he is taking on. The wonderful job he was able to do on behalf of hundreds of students who passed through his hands as headmaster at Pickering college is something which, to my mind, recommends him highly for the onerous duties he has now taken on as one of the commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I should like to answer some questions that have been asked by speakers this afternoon. Perhaps it will not be possible for me to answer them all, but I think I can cover them fairly well.
In the first place, I think I should say something about the operations of the commissioner of penitentiaries during the past year. The foundation for the program being followed in the operation of the penitentiary system is to be found in the report of the present commissioner of penitentiaries, which I think was circulated in February of 1947. That was the report referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Selkirk. To some extent that

report is based upon the Archambault report, but does not go the length recommended by the Archambault report; that is, the centralization of control of all penal institutions in the dominion government. That probably is not practicable. We have no reason whatever to think it is practicable. We have had no request for anything of that kind from any of the provinces with the exception of two, I think I am safe in saying; those are the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba. While I have stated in this house that if the provinces wished us to give consideration to this important change in the constitution of our penitentiary system we would do so, I do not anticipate that I shall get any request to give consideration to it, having in mind the acri-moniuos speeches which have been made in some parts of Canada about the desire of the dominion government to centralize authority here in Ottawa.
So we are proceeding on a different footing, the one set out in General Gibson's report of February, 1947. I should like to tell the committee some of the things that have been done during the past year. The new act was proclaimed on September 1, 1947. The administration was reorganized. General Gibson was appointed commissioner, and two deputy commissioners, Mr. McCulley and Doctor Gendreau, were appointed. There are three assistant commissioners, the senior assistant commissioner being Mr. Sauvant. A training school for officers was inaugurated, and the second course is now in progress. The courses are given at Rockcliffe, in the R.C.M.P. barracks there. Twenty-five of the personnel of the penitentiaries come in for each course, which lasts six weeks. I visited this school being carried on there under the guidance or control or direction of Mr. McCulley, and found the atmosphere to be excellent. In other words, those who come in from the penitentiaries are keen to learn all they can. The instructors seem very good. There is not the slightest evidence of any feeling that this is a holiday or a lark or anything like that. They are very much in earnest about learning what they can about how to carry on their duties in the penitentiaries.
The salaries have been revised in all grades. In the course of his remarks the hon. member for Selkirk said that the cost of living had increased by 50 per cent or thereabouts, and that the remuneration of the employees of the penitentiaries branch had not been increased to the same extent. But the remuneration has increased by approximately 50 per cent since 1939 in all except the highest grades. For guards the 1939 range was from
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
SI,200 to $1,500 a year. After a recent increase, I think more recent than the last one with which the hon. member is familiar, and certainly more recent than the rate in existence last January, when the hon. member for New Westminster spoke to me about the matter, the 1948 range for guards is from $1,800 to $2,100, with a higher maximum than that for twenty per cent of the guards.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Are they not also supplied with clothing and uniforms and shoes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Yes, they are.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: So they really get more than the amounts mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Yes. They also get a free meal in the middle of the day and free medical services.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: And some pension rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
And superannuation, rights
under exactly the same system as the civil service, which I cannot help reiterating is an extremely generous superannuation system, judged by any standard at all. The increases over the 1939 rates in the other grades are as follows:
Keeper	
Instructor	
Chief keeper ... Chief trade instr. Warden, grade 1 Warden, grade 2

2.400-	2,700
2.700-	3,300
2.700-	3,300 4.800- 5,400
5.400-	6,000
During the past year there has been an important, rapid extension of the system of classification. We have spoken in this house about the importance, first, of classification of prisoners, and, then, of segregation. I am prepared to admit that the segregation has not been carried on to the extent that ultimately it should be, because so much construction is required. There just are not the buildings and the facilities. The more you finally segregate, the more facilities you require, of course; but progress is being made in segregation, and more progress will be made in future when labour and material for construction become more readily available. First, however, there has to be classification. Classification officers have now been appointed in all the penitentiaries, and a proper system of classification is being developed.
Full-time vocational training has been inaugurated for young convicts at Collin's Bay and St. Vincent de Paul penitentiaries, where they receive instruction in construction carpentry, cabinet making, brick masonry, plumbing and steamfitting, tinsmithing and drafting. That system of full-time vocational
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: For the housing of guards?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Yes, for guards' houses. Therefore that is being taken- care of.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I am pleased to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: The hon. member for Selkirk has repeated the complaint he has made on other -occasions with -respect t-o the pension system. His point is that certain persons have to keep on paying in som-e cases until they have paid in more than they could possibly get out.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I have three cases I shall send to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
All- right; I would like to see them. H-owever, all I can say is that the rule being applied t-o these penitentiary employees is -exactly the same as the on-e applied throughout the civil service. There is no difference whatever. I wish to reiterate that the Civil Service Superannuation Act is an exceedingly liberal act.
It may be that if a person has to pay up -arrears and is given the option of paying a lump sum or paying so much for life, he will pay m-ore by taking the latter option, if he lives long -enough. But he w-ill not pay anything at all if he dies very soon.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Let us be reasonable about this. These people were temporaries who became permanent. As temporaries they were not entitled to superannuation. They

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
were given the privilege of paying for the back period which would partly-and only partly-pay the cost of their receiving a pension, or their families receiving pensions. They had the option of paying that up, with about one-third of the cost to the government. They could not do that, so it was said to them, "All right, instead of paying a lump sum, you may pay so much a year for the rest of your life." Well, the person who does that takes a chance of losing by living too long. There is no doubt about that. However that cannot be avoided. It is an option, and a fair option, based upon actuarial principles.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: These men could not be temporary employees, because they were in the service since 1921.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: There are people who have been temporaries for many years. Finally they become permanent. My officials instruct me that these people did not elect to take advantage of the superannuation act. Then later in 1944, they elected to take advantage of the act.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: When some of those people are sixty-eight years of age they will have paid compound interest on all they owe the government, and still they have to pay to the end of their days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I am satisfied my hon. friend is unreasonable in the position he takes. We are talking about these civil servants or penitentiary employees who were given a year or two years in 1924 or 1925 to exercise the option. They did not exercise it. But they found out twenty years later that it would have been advantageous for them to exercise it. Then they are given another opportunity to exercise it, provided that they pay up the arrears. They are given the option of paying a lump sum or of paying on an actuarial basis. If they find there is more money taken away from them if they go on that basis, they have no complaint.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I hope the minister does not really mean that-that I am unreasonable- because I think I am the most reasonable man in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Usually, yes.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I have indicated this
grievance, and I would be failing in my duty if I did not bring it to the attention of the committee. These men have a just grievance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: All right; we shall let it go at that.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to mention the hours; is it fifty-one hours?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Forty-eight hours, I believe.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Do you not think it should be 'less than that?
Mr. ILS'LEY: If it is less than that you have to lock the prisoners up earlier.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: There are lots of men in the country now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: It is difficult to arrange the shifts.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: That was the excuse made during the war, that there were not sufficient men. There are plenty of men now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Well, it is forty-eight hours a week.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Would the minister answer a question on the point he has been arguing with the hon. member for Selkirk? The minister said that in 1921 these guards who were temporary employees had the option of coming under the superannuation scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: I think I am wrong in that. I thought the hon. member was talking about temporaries. He was talking about permanents who were given the privilege of coming under the superannuation act in 1924 but who elected not to do so.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: As temporaries they would not have that option.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: No, they would not have it as temporaries.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Is it not unreasonable to keep people in the service for twenty-five or thirty years, classify them as temporaries and deprive them of that privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
These people were not. That is another question.
Then the hon. member for Davenport asked what was being done by way of reclamation. I believe I have answered that pretty thoroughly. Our whole policy is directed toward reform by all the methods I have mentioned. As I say, arrangements are made with the John Howard societies to get in contact with them upon their release from the penitentiaries, and the estimates provide for grants to the John Howard societies.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Do they get them jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
The prisoners' aid societies do the best they can to place them.
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: The minister will remember that I said I had exercised myself in obtaining jobs for those whom I knew. They have done very well, because I do not know of any who have relapsed. How much does a prisoner take out of a penitentiary in his pocket when he is released? When he is out of money, what does he do for more?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: It is not less than $10, and it depends upon the length of time he has been in the penitentiary.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: That would not take him anywhere. Much of the trouble comes from a lack of supervision over the prisoner after he is released. I do not know how it can be done, but certainly $10 would hardly take him from Kingston to Toronto, even riding in a second-class car. When he gets to Toronto he may need some place to lie down in, because they do not all have homes to go to. Then he must eat. There should be some place where a released prisoner feels he can go to obtain aid. This would not be mollycoddling; it is simply a matter of keeping them from going out and robbing some home or knocking somebody down on the street and taking their money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
The average cash taken out is $18 and transportation is paid to the place of sentence. The John Howard societies are communicated with to see if they cannot help to get these men established.
The hon. member for Lake Centre said something about pay, but I think I have answered that. Then he said there was no permanency. These men have the same permanency as civil servants, except that they can be dismissed by the minister for cause, while a permanent civil servant can be dismissed for cause, only by the governor in council. They have the same rights under the supeiannuation fund as civil servants.
The hon. member for Lake Centre wanted to know how arms get into the penitentiaries. The only recent instance is that at Kingston when a revolver got into the penitentiary. It is not known how, but the matter is under investigation.
The hon. member for Lake Centre said that the remission service was unsatisfactory. We do not get many complaints about the remission service, but it may be susceptible of some improvement.
The hon. member for Fort William asked whether I am in favour of letting out a convict whose record is good when someone will sponsor him? Our whole remission service is based on those principles which are pretty consistently applied.

The hon. member for New Westminster asked if I was acquainted with the investigations of a royal commission in Great Britain into the Borstal system. I am not, but I believe I read somewhere that the figures with reference to the Borstal system are not quite as satisfactory today as they were some years ago. There has been a little deterioration, not in the system, but in the results from the system.
I thank the hon. member for Eglinton for the tribute he has paid to Mr. McCulley, one of the deputy commissioners. I think everyone agrees that it was a good appointment, as was also the appointment of Doctor Gendreau. I need hardly say that the same would apply to the appointment of the commissioner.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
I should like to call the attention of the minister to three or four matters. I am greatly dissatisfied with the inspection of these institutions. You are spending large sums of money, six to seven million dollars a year, and getting little value in. the way of prison reform. The other evening I referred to the fact that in the old country they had had real law reform. Half of the prisons over there have been closed under the summary offenders act.
What prison reform has there been since the Archambault report? I venture to say that inspection is one of the most important functions you have, and there is no inspection except by crown officers. These institutions, whether they are rightly or wrongly managed, have been criticized by some of the superior court judges of the provinces. It is one of the cardinal principles of Magna Carta that the people shall take a large share in the administration of criminal justice. These institutions are managed only by crown officers, and the motto over their doors should be, "Abandon hope all ye who enter here".
As I say, there is no inspection except by crown officers. I had a bill up the other night for consideration. I want to compliment the minister on the amount of time he has given to this service since he took charge of the department. While I do not think the changes made go as far as they should, I want to say that he has done a great deal to bring these institutions to the attention of the public. He is one attorney general who has done this. I know that some never paid any attention to this branch of the department and were never in these places to see what was going on.
I should like to see these institutions inspected by businessmen because these places are extremely important. I remember when

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
we were appointing a new chief constable in Toronto a deputation, including Sir John Eaton, asked that a soldier be appointed. I said to them, "Can you learn how to run a department in Eaton's in a day? How are you going to learn this police business in a day? How are you going to learn the police or penal institution business in a day?" That just cannot be done. You must be in the business all your life to know about it.
I believe that applies as far as possible to this department, but there should be a proper system of inspection. Hon. members of the House of Commons have been on the board of visitors for years, but how many in this chamber have been in any of these institutions to see what is going on? I know the hon. member for Davenport is one who has visited one of these places. Years ago the only reform in these institutions was by a Conservative government in Ontario under Sir James Whitney, and by our city of Toronto, a pioneer city in prison reform, which built in 1910-11 two jail farms, one for men on Yonge street and one for women three miles away at Concord.
We have an old jail down on the Don which is in my constituency. It was built about the time of confederation and what I am saying here to this government applies to that institution. The former hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers), and another hon. member looked into these institutions, and the construction inside them is against all the known laws of public hygiene, and the member for St. Mary said the same thing. There should be some better system of inspection and the public should know what is going on inside these institutions. You can. never inspect them by sitting in your office. True, we have a very fine commissioner in charge of the penitentiaries. We have commissions on everything now. Everybody is changing his title. You change the name but you do not change the system. Under the present system you cannot find out what is going on in the penitentiaries, and we want to know and the public want to know. The Archam-bault report recommended that there should be a better system of conducting these penitentiaries. Every great war is followed by unrest, especially among the younger people who have travelled through difficult days, and the penitentiary population increases.
I should like to make the following suggestions to the minister. I do not want to hold up his estimates, because he has been very patient not only regarding private bills but the whole system of penitentiary and justice administration. The public are very much dis-5849-315*
satisfied with the conduct of some of these institutions. We have not the system which we should have, especially for youthful offenders. It is many years since the Archambault report was brought down. It grew out of debates on these institutions in this house. The commission recommended many changes. It is true that some minor changes which have been made are listed in the back of the report of the present commissioner of penitentiaries. I admit that considerable changes have been made, and so far so good; but they are not sufficient, especially at a time like this when people are being sentenced for minor infractions of the control laws. Can you blame anybody from trying to escape from these institutions? The penalty is too great-no wonder there are escapees.
I wrote to some of the wardens a few- years ago and I found that very little visiting of these institutions was done. Why not have the grand jury or even the petit jury inspect these institutions. Jury inspection has been the system in the province of Ontario ever since confederation. Why should the jury inspection system not apply to federal institutions? The jury would not go there to criticize the institutions but would strengthen the hand of the present commissioner. I do not say that they should go to these institutions more than once or twice a year, because in some provinces there are no grand juries and in others the petit juries are reduced to five in number. But undoubtedly w-e need a more adequate inspection system. That was urged in the report of Mr. Justice Archambault, and it was supported by the late Chief Justice Meredith, who tried more cases out on circuit at the assizes for more than fifty years than any other judge in Ontario or Canada. Many judges have emphasized the value of an inspection of these institutions, municipal, provincial and dominion, by juries, and I hope that something along that line will be done. It is the key to law reform. The public should be made aware of what is going on in these institutions. Some punishments are entirely too drastic, so much so that one would think we were living in the middle ages.
I want to thank the minister for the manner in which he has received my suggestions, in the same spirit as that in which I have made them. I am not criticizing the present commissioner. He has had a distinguished career in another sphere of activity, and it may be that in the years to come he may do good work in the penitentiaries; but the public believe that prison reform, which they had in Great Britain twenty-five years ago, is altogether too slow in coming in Canada.

I have a return here, No. 167, which shows a property sold by the Department of Transport. It shows lots 122, 123 and 124, concession 1, west Yonge street, Toronto, twenty-one acres, sold for $105, although it cost the government $430, and I have information showing that property in that neighbourhood is selling and has sold at $400 or more an acre. I would ask the minister why this land was sold for less than it cost the government away back in 1907 to 1911. Despite the fact that the return says this land was sold by tender, I have reliable information that no tenders were called at all. I would like a little information on that.
Where is the land?

Lots 122, 123 and 124, concession 1, west Yonge street, Toronto. It was part of the land that was bought by the government from 1907 to 1911 for the Newmarket branch of the Trent canal. The information I have here shows that the land around it has been selling at $400 an acre, and some as high as $500 an acre.

I do not remember the details of this particular sale. It is somewhat vague in my memory now, but my recollection is that it was advertised. It may be that there were no bids and that, later on, the land was sold privately, but I should not like to be committed to that statement. I shall look into the matter and give my hon. friend a reply before I am through with my estimates.

Even if it were sold privately, those who sold it should have checked on the property nearby and should not have sold it for $5 an acre. That was giving it

away. This is valuable land. The property around there is now all built up with houses.
I remember now; it was advertised on more than one occasion. There were bids in certain instances and in others there were not.
That was other land round there.
What happened was, I think, that the land was put together in a block and sold. In any event, I shall get the information for my hon. friend.
Has the minister a report as to the extent of the damage done to the Canadian National railway lines by the floods in British Columbia? What is the estimated cost of repairs?
I gave that information in much detail on the orders of the day.
Today?
I gave a complete statement on it on Monday, I think.
