467. Canals-construction and improvements, $579,660.

I spoke about this matter last year and at other times when the estimates were up. The Rideau canal, and also the Trent canal have great attractions for United States tourists; but, owing to the fact that so many automobiles are used these days, the steamers which we used to have on these canals are not running today. Therefore the weeds are allowed to grow in the rivers and the lakes of the canals. Many of the little docks that the government put in years ago are of no use today, on account of the fact that the entrance from a lake or from the canal itself is blocked with weeds. Would it not be possible, and would it not be good business on the part of the government, to clear these weeds out of these sections, because in Canada, and especially in my district, the ICawartha district, we depend on the tourist for a great deal of business. We depend on them for United States dollars, and it is the United States tourist who is asking that these weeds be taken out of these channels. If the department had a weed cutter it would not cost very much to do the job. The excuse given to me last year was that if the department cut the weeds they would float ashore and create a menace, breed flies and so on. That condition would prevail for only a couple of days and then it would be over. If the

Supply*-Transport
weeds were cut, growth would be kept down. Another way of doing away with them around the docks is, of course, to put lime down. That keeps them down for perhaps two or three years, and I do not think it affects the fish at all. Something should be done in that regard. We spend $650,000 or more advertising for United States tourists, and we should do everything possible for their convenience when they get here.

The last time my hon. friend brought this matter up, I think the difficulty was that these weeds w'ere not in navigable channels. They were in close to the dock or close to a channel which took care of boats of small draft. There are perhaps 500 miles or more of secondary canals, not all of which are of tourist value. Because of that, it would not be a simple matter in so far as the work and the costs are concerned. It might not be a big job to cut the weeds in the channels to which my hon. friend refers, but the whole question is whether it is a responsibility of the Department of Transport. If we were to cut them there, by inference it would create an obligation to cut them elsewhere. I am not saying that it cannot be done or that it will not be done, that is the objection which occurred to me when my hon. friend brought the matter up. I told him that I would ask my officers to look into it. They did, and they came to the conclusion that they would be assuming an obligation to cut the weeds in the other places as well. I do not know that the position has changed since, but I shall be glad to ask my people to look at it again.

Take the case of Keene, Ontario. There is a government dock at Keene on the river that runs from Keene into Rice lake, which is only a short stretch. That dock was built at Keene by the government. Thousands of United States tourists go there. They come into the Rice lake district, 'winter, summer, spring and fall, but they can hardly use an outboard motor in that section today from the main canal in Rice lake up to the Keene dock. The dock is there. It was built when the steamboats were operating. The steamboats kept it clear, but an outboard motor cannot plow through there. It is not only for the convenience of the United States tourists who are there but also for the business people in the section. They need the business of these tourists. In many cases the tourists have to go up the river to Keene to get their mail, because some of them have no roads or they are on an island. They have to go by boat for their mail, but they cannot go all the way. They have to paddle
through those weeds. There are not 500 miles' of weeds which would have to be cleared..
There is another spot which should be cleared. It has been checked by the superintendent of the department in Peterborough, Mr. Ryan. I refer to Little lake. Weeds have grown in Little lake because of the dam and the locks below. There is a concrete dock and shed and everything on George street, right on Little lake, but to get from the main canal you have to go through weeds. The weeds in that section are a menace to the outboard motor and to health, I would say, because they stop the proper flow of water down that stream.

May I add a word, because I have exactly the same situation in Muskoka outside the town of Bracebridge? It seems to me that the situation described by the hon. member for Peterborough West is something that somebody has to deal with; otherwise an impossible situation will be created, and many of these waterways will fill up and become unusable for local inhabitants, and what is more important, for the tourists. I am not quite clear as to the responsibility in these matters. The waters referred to by my hon. friend, and certainly the waters that I have in mind, are navigable waters. Am I right in assuming that the department has a responsibility there? If I am, then the minister will answer me.
I can answer that right away.
May I first just ask a supplementary question? If the department is not responsible, then is it a matter of individual initiative for the riparian owner?

To answer the first question on navigable waters, the department has a responsibility with reference to aids to navigation and the keeping open of the channel; but it has no statutory responsibility with reference to the cutting of weeds.
What is meant by "the keeping open of the channel"?
Keeping it open in the sense of having proper beacons, lights and aids to navigation to permit traffic to go from one end of the waterway to the other.

But the minister would not suggest that that is what happened between Montreal and
Supply-Transport

Quebec? The department or whoever has the responsibility there keeps the channel open, free and available for the passage of traffic.
That is another matter altogether. From Montreal to Quebec it is a matter of dredging.

Is a different principle involved there? Between Montreal and Quebec there is the responsibility to keep the channel open. At first blush, the minister's answer does not seem to be a good one, because actually between Montreal and Quebec much more has to be done than is suggested by us. I take it that it would be a much more difficult task to do dredging than it would be to cut weeds. I cannot yet see that the minister has given an answer to my question. If this is a navigable stream and particularly, as my hon. friend has said, where you have built wharves, is it not your responsibility to provide access to them? On the analogy of the situation between Montreal and Quebec, surety it is.

There is a distinction between the two. From Montreal to Quebec the department has dredged the channel to a certain depth-I think it is thirty-five feet- in order to keep it open for ships of certain draft. On the canal to which the hon. member for Peterborough refers, the situation is different. We do not usually take responsibility for cutting weeds on canals. We cut weeds on government property, on canal banks and the like. But cutting weeds for tourist purposes is not an obligation of the Department of Transport.
It should be.
My hon. friend says it should be. That is another matter. With deference, I submit that it should not be. However, I shall be glad to have the matter looked into further.

I may perhaps be stupid, but it seems to me that the minister has not at all explained to me this distinction. In each of these cases you have a navigable water. In the one case, as the minister has pointed out, the department has assumed responsibility for keeping open a channel thirty-five feet in depth, and it acts accordingly. In these other cases, particularly where a canal has been built or at any rate where there is a navigable water of which the department has charge-and which, as the minister says, has navigating lights where necessary-and still more so where wharves have been built to which access has

been had, surety the minister does not say there is no responsibility there. What is the difference in principle between cutting weeds and dredging out clay or whatever it is? I cannot follow that distinction.
I am sorry if I am not making myself clear, but I hope I am rvhen I state that there is no responsibility in the Department of Transport, as I understand it, to keep the water clear of weeds.

I am sorry to persist; but why does the minister distinguish between weeds, let us say, and stones, clay or sand? What is the distinction? In the St. Lawrence you recognize that you must keep the channel clear. Why not in the Muskoka river? What is the difference?
The difference is as I have stated. The responsibility of the department is to keep the channel open for commercial traffic and not for tourist traffic.
Oh, that is a new point. Is that in the act? Surety a navigable stream is a navigable stream, and surety if you build wharves you have some responsibility to assure access to them.

We do not build wharves in the Department of Transport. That is not our responsibility. We have never built wharves in the Department of Transport. They were built by others. We operate the wharves once they are built.

All right. The minister must not become too legalistic on me, because he is better at that kind of thing than I am. Let us get back to the point. Let me retract what I said about the department's building wharves. Will the minister say whether I am correct in thinking that those wharves are dominion government property?
That, is right.
And am I correct in thinking that it is the duty of his department to maintain access to them? Is that correct?
That is correct.
If weeds impede access to them, is it not your duty to take out the weeds?

I do not think weeds impede the access of ships bringing trade and commerce to a port. That is my understand-

Supply-Transport
mg of the situation. But that is not the point which the hon. member for Peterborough raised. He raised the point that weeds are impeding tourist craft and boats of that kind from coming in. He mentioned the stretch from Keene to Rice lake. I do not know just what the position of the channel is there. I am not familiar with that.
It is about a mile long.
Is it on canal property?
It was originally, yes.
It is probably connecting one canal with another.

Rice lake runs from Hastings up to Bewdley, and Keene is on the north part of it, with the Indian river running down. The dock is up in there. Years ago all kinds of boats went up in there, including steamboats. Later on, there were launches. First there were naphtha launches and then gasoline ones. A gasoline launch cannot go up there now, because it would get tied up in the weeds.
It is not a navigable channel.
It was.
It is not a navigable channel in the sense that ships bringing in a cargo come in there. How many feet deep is the channel?

It would be as deep as you can make it. In some places the Trent canal has a clearance of six feet and in other places a clearance of nine feet. There would be no reason why you could not have a clearance of nine feet in there if you want it. Steamships 100 feet or more in length used to go up in there. At many other spots such as Harwood, Gore's Landing and Bewdley, the weeds should be cleared out. As I said before, thousands of tourists are going up in there. We are spending $650,000 or more to advertise for United States tourists. We must do everything possible to look after their interests when they get here. They are buying outboard motors which are manufactured in Peterborough. We want them to use those outboard motors. We want to keep the working men in Canada busy. We want to keep our plants going.

I wish to add something to what the hon. member has said. I really do not believe the minister can seriously say that the department's responsibility is to keep these channels open only for a certain type of craft and that the summer craft, such as launches and so on, are to be distinguished from what I think the
minister implied were more the commercial type of craft. In the broad sense, these summer craft are just as commercial as anything in the world could be, because they provide a great deal of business in the district. It is an obvious fact, as obvious as it can be, that if these waters become impassable, it may be a great detriment to the whole area. It is clear to me that these weeds must be kept down. The minister's argument that the department is not responsible for that seems to me, if I have understood him correctly, to be untenable; because what he says is apparently that weeds must be treated in a different way from the more solid obstacles which he removes in order to keep the channels open. I cannot believe that the minister intends to say this summer traffic, which, after all, is important to that whole area, is to be disregarded and that, in so far as the department is concerned, these waterways with docks on them which are government property are to be allowed virtually to become impassable. I cannot believe he intends to take that position, and yet that seems to be what he has said.
I should like to send this document over to the minister. It is entitled 'Waters to explore-the Trent." It is interesting, and I know it will be quite an education to him.
I have seen it, but I shall be glad to look at it again.

I hope the minister will look into this weed cutting, because it means thousands of dollars to the people of Ontario.
While we are on this item of canals, I should like to mention once more the eyesore which still confronts us when we come into Ottawa, in connection with the concrete retaining walls of the Rideau canal. The department is doing some work on the walls, and I was wondering if that work would be continued until all the walls are straightened out and patched up where they were eaten away, and so on, and the banks fixed up. It is a very pretty spot, but it needs to be improved.

We are proceeding piecemeal with the repairs to the retaining wall to which my hon. friend refers. Last year we did some work; this year we are doing more. I believe a portion of the work is now complete, and there is an item of $25,000 in the estimates to provide for the continuation of this work.
That is only a fleabite.

It may be only a fleabite, but we must proceed gradually. I think we have done very well in the last two years. A considerable amount of work remains to be done, and we propose to do it.

I should like to ask the minister what provision is made for the removal of debris from the canals. I am now drawing attention to a condition in the Trent canal near the village of Frankford, directly in front of dam No. 6. A large amount of debris, presumably stone, covering an area of half an acre or more, has been deposited in the river, causing the main current of the stream to turn to the west and run over private property, damaging good garden land, the owner of which is not very well pleased. It seems to me that it would not be very hard to remove this material, because it is all loose. It was deposited there during high water. Probably the stone was raised up by frost and brought down, and it has been left in the middle of the stream in front of the dam.

I believe the hon. gentleman brought this matter to my attention last year. The position is that the equipment required to get rid of the debris to which lie refers has not been available. We have it on hand now, however, and it is hoped that we may be able to remedy the situation during the course of the summer.

Just in that connection, the man who owns the land told me, after I had been in consultation with the minister, that some official of the department came there and wanted him to sell his land. That official did not say anything about improving the condition.

I would hesitate to believe that an officer of the department would go there and ask this man to sell his land. If he did so, he was certainly acting outside his authority. I would not think that a proper thing for an officer of the department to do.
I found it rather peculiar at the time; but the owner of the land is a responsible resident of the village of Frankford, and I would have every confidence in anything he told me.

This item provides an amount of $579,660, and the total of the items under canal service is $3,886,408. I want to point out to the committee that these expenditures are made almost entirely in central Canada. We in the maritime provinces have been overlooked pretty much since confederation. We have one canal project with which I am sure the minister is familiar, though I do not know that he has done much about it. I refer to the Chignecto canal.
Those of us coming from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have brought this matter before the house on different occasions since that canal and ship railway were projected. A subsidy was voted by parliament; and earlier in the session I made the estimate that if the money voted had been placed to our credit at compound interest it would amount by now to well on to $15,000,000. A subsidy for the completion of the Chignecto canal was cancelled for financial reasons; the builders were not able to complete their work within the time specified.
We do not object to these canals in central Canada, and we realize that it is necessary to maintain them. They are used for transportation purposes. With the canals, the river services and the lake services, manufacturers and shippers in central Canada are able to get cheap transportation. The railways have put competitive rates into effect, and this portion of Canada gets the advantage. We have no canals, though we are entitled to them; we have no such competitive rates, so that we have to pay the regular freight rates.
In view of our claims; in view of the fact that this undertaking was being dealt with before confederation and at the time of confederation; in view of the fact that a subsidy was voted in order to provide this service across the isthmus of Chignecto, I ask the minister and his department to take some action to advance the project. I ask him to see that surveys and estimates are prepared, and that a practical investigation is carried out as to the cost today. The maritime board of trade, the maritime mayors, members of parliament, newspapers and so on in recent months have been placing before the minister and the public the claims of that part of Canada for some consideration; and I make another appeal today. Since I have been here,
I have brought up this matter on many occasions, and again I ask the minister and his department to deal seriously with this question and to take some action, so that we may have the benefit of modem transportation facilities across the isthmus of Chignecto.

I rise to second the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland. It is not necessary to speak at length at this time, because this matter has been raised on numerous occasions by members from the maritime provinces. I must say, however, I cannot find myself shedding any tears for the failure to remove obsolete canals in Ontario, so long as canals are being neglected in the maritime provinces. It was all veiy well for Ontario to have pleasure excursions, scenic beauty and places for the boys to go swimming, but we in the maritime provinces are asking for canals which would be of some benefit to the maritime provinces and to the whole of Canada.
As the hon. member for Cumberland has pointed out, the rest of Canada, particularly Ontario, owes the maritime provinces a great debt, so far as canals are concerned. Those canals in Ontario were not built by the province; they were built by the federal government, and the maritime provinces contributed many millions of dollars. Now that those canals have become obsolete, and when at the same time there is an opportunity to build a canal which would be of some commercial benefit to the country, I suggest that some of this $4,000,000 be taken to construct the Ohignecto canal, which I sincerely believe would be of great benefit to the whole country.
This matter has been before the house on many occasions and has been discussed by all members from the maritime provinces. As the hon. member for Cumberland has stated, our press has given a clear outline of the possibilities, and the great help such a construction would be to commerce in this country.
One of the finest things the Minister of Transport could do would be to begin construction of the Chignecto canal. If he were to do so, I know his name would go down in the history of our part of the country and, I believe, the rest of Canada, as being a most efficient minister in his department.

I have heard of a game in which, if you hold two cards of the same kind, and then add another, your position is considerably strengthened, I am not as familiar with that game as some others might be, but in this instance when two aces are showing I should like to add my strength, and to put in my word for further consideration of this project.
In the past I have not urged this to any great extent, because I considered there were some features which might not be entirely in the interests of certain sections of Canada. I am always a little careful in connection with disturbing interests certain sections hold. I have in mind particularly the shipping of the
great port of Halifax. I can see where, at great expense, the proposals now made might operate to the detriment of Halifax.
At the same time I am in accord with the thoughts expressed by the hon. members for Cumberland and Royal, and I hope the minister will look into the matter to ascertain whether this would be a wise expenditure, and whether the project is feasible. Anything the minister can do in connection with this or any other project which will help transportation and give us greater possibilities in trade with central Canada should be looked into.

I rise to support what has been said by the hon. members for Cumberland and Royal in connection with the building of the canal. If that canal service is put through, perhaps it would be of greater benefit to the farmers of Prince Edward Island than to any other group in Canada, and especially in the maritime provinces. Therefore I gladly endorse what the hon. members have said.
The minister has just said there is a revenue of about a million dollars from the canals. I notice that the remaining expenditures are not charged up as a deficit, but that they appear in the public accounts as a service. I would draw to the minister's attention the different circumstances which apply to the ferry service to Prince Edward Island, which is a much greater revenue producer than are the canals. When the accounts are balanced a deficit is charged against Prince Edward Island, or against the service. I say it should appear in the public accounts in the same manner as this is shown, namely a service paid by the federal treasury.
I would endeavour to impress this upon the minister, so that at another time when public accounts are being made up, the word "deficit" would be deleted, where it applies in respect of the ferry system between Borden and Tormentine, and that it should appear as a canal service. It is a service which we purchased in 1873 and for which we paid highly. Why should it now be charged as a deficit?

I should like to have a statement from the minister. When we sit opposite him we get the impression that he understands the representations we make, and that he is in sympathy with us. If his name is identified with the construction of the Chignecto canal he will have shown his, administrative capacity and his control of his department.
The matter has been discussed today by hon. members from the maritime provinces, and I shall not be content with only a smile or a good-will greeting from the minister.

I want a statement from him in which he sets out his attitude toward the construction of the Chignecto canal, always keeping in mind the three or four hundred million dollars already expended in central Canada, and the further fact that in the estimates now before us there is an appropriation of $3,886,408 for the canal service. What is the minister's attitude toward the Chignecto canal?

The hon. member has inquired about two things. His first question was whether all the sum voted for canal purposes, operation and maintenance, is in respect of canals in Ontario and Quebec. The answer is yes, with the exception of a small expenditure of about $20,000 on the St. Peter's canal in the maritime provinces.
With reference to the Chignecto canal, the hon. member has made representations about this before, and he made them again this year on these estimates. Representations have been made also by the hon. member for Royal.
All I can say is that I have received many representations from bodies in the maritime provinces, and that I am sympathetic to these representations. No minister of transport who has at heart the opening up of transportation facilities could be anything but sympathetic. However I have to look at the position as I find it on the record. The hon. member unquestionably knows that down through the years many surveys and reports have been made concerning the advisability, the feasibility and the economic advantages and disadvantages of constructing the Chignecto canal. Surveys were made as far back as 1822, and I think there have been eight or ten altogether.
When was the most recent one made?

In 1931. That was made by virtue of an order in council appointing a commission to inquire into the Chignecto canal project. I have the report before me, and the recommendation on page 11 reads:
Having regard to transport facilities already available in the maritimes area, we cannot see where any interest would suffer were the Chignecto canal project to be permitted to stand in abeyance until it can be further examined in the light of future developments in Canada's economic situation.
What is the date of that?

1931. Of course that recommendation was not detrimental or opposed to the building of a canal; it simply stated as a conclusion that, having regard to Ml the circumstances, the commission could
rMr. Black (CumberHnd).]
not see where any interest would suffer if the matter were allowed to stand.
That was at the height of the depression.

That was many years ago, in 1931. It may well be that economic conditions have changed to such an extent that another survey would be warranted. The hon. member suggests that we begin construction immediately, but I think he will agree with me that, before that is done, we should look at it by way of a survey or investigation along the lines of that carried on previously and having regard to the position as it now is. I am not prepared to state that it is possible to do that at this time, neither am I prepared to state that we would not do it. However, I can say that I shall be glad to look into the matter again in the light of the position as we find it now. I would have to consult my colleagues in the government to ascertain whether it would be advisable to appoint another commission to see if, because of changed conditions, it would be practical to consider the construction of the Chignecto canal.

As one friendly to any proposal which will assist in the economic advance of the maritime provinces, I am glad to hear what the minister said a moment ago, that the matter of the Chignecto canal will be looked into again. He said it had been discussed since 1931, but it goes back much farther than that. I was interested in reading some of the reports made in the early days 'of the French regime. The French administrators strongly recommended to their government in Paris that a canal be cut across the isthmus.
A couple of years ago I had the pleasure of covering more or less all that area in company with the hon. member for Cumberland. There are many good vantage points from which one can see the isthmus, and I remember remarking at the time that the early French pioneers deserved a lot of credit for the vision they had.
There have been many engineering advances made since the last report was presented. I read over the report; in fact I took it with me on my last survey of the isthmus. While it would not be the easiest engineering feat to perform, it can be performed. Our United States friends had a somewhat similar problem in connection with the canal they cut across the Cape Cod isthmus. One of their main engineering problems was to keep the sides from falling in, but they overcame that. Another problem was caused by the six-foot tides. During one portion of the day there

Supply[DOT]-Transport
would be six-foot tides at the west end of the canal, while for the other portion of the day there would be six-foot tides at the east end.
They overcame all the difficulties, and that canal is now providing a fine service. It is a good commercial canal, and they have a couple of large bridges which lift up to let ships go through., but it is also of strategic importance. I doubt very much, if the United States had to do it over again, they would wait as long to build that canal as they did.
The Chignecto canal would not be only a commercial canal; it would be of strategic value to Canada. It would render great service to commerce in the bay of Fundy and to "the island." The hon. member for Queens will not listen to anyone who calls it anything but "the island." Everyone is supposed to know what is meant when you say "the island." It is a beautiful island. If the canal were opened up it would bring Charlottetown much closer to Boston and by a route that would be comparatively safe. Has the minister been across the isthmus?
Yes.
I would like to be there with him if he is going again.
The hon. member followed me quite closely on his last trip.

I think we were there about the same time. It is an intensely interesting trip, especially to anyone interested in engineering. The Cape Cod canal is about fifteen miles long and it takes much larger ships than it is proposed would pass through the Chignecto canal. Then the United States propose building a sea-level canal across the Panama isthmus. Anyone interested in the building of the Chignecto canal would find many things of great value in the engineering works proposed for the new Panama canal. In order to take care of tides that run as high as tw'enty feet on the west side, they propose building a gigantic lock dock. On the west side, ships entering from the Pacific ocean, say on a twenty-foot rise of tide, would be lowered down to the canal level in the lock dock and sail to the east side of the isthmus; and similarly boats travelling west would enter the lock dock and remain until they could get out into the Pacific ocean. Some such lock dock as that would be necessary, I am satisfied, in connection with the Chignecto canal. If I remember correctly, an engineer-I have forgotten his name-did plan building a railway across the isthmus and he projected the route. I went over it, and I have nothing but praise for those who engineered that route, which was for the
purpose of taking ships across on a railway. The proposal was to build an entrance lock dock on the west side, into which the ship would rise up and go down with the rise and fall of the tide.
To close the argument, I assure the minister that I shall be glad to support any estimate he brings in for building the Chignecto canal and will be as much help to him and to whoever has to do with the proposed works as I can be. I am firmly convinced that a canal across the Chignecto isthmus would be a great thing for the maritime provinces. It would mean, for instance, that ships could load up on the bay of Fundy with Joggins coal or Springhill coal. They would not need to be ships of a capacity to go out into the ocean, but 2,000 to 5,000 tonners, which could load up on the bay of Fundy, sail through that canal and go right up to Montreal and Toronto. It would be a great thing for us, too, in the central provinces, because we would load the ships up with products to send back to the maritimes, so that there would be commerce both ways. I hope that the minister will look into the matter carefully and consider also the strategical angle. This country is becoming more and more interested in international affairs and if it ever became embroiled in another world war, just fancy what the Chignecto canal would mean to our warships and to United States battleships coming to assist us in the defence of the gulf of the St. Lawrence. The minister should take up that question with the defence department and invite them to come in and help build the canal not only as a commercial canal but also as a strategic canal.

The Trent valley canal is more important today than it ever was dreamt of being forty years ago. I can show the minister tourist resorts along the Trent valley canal, in which a great deal of money has been invested and which are bringing more money into Canada in one year than w'as thought of as possible in ten years, some forty years ago. There is a lot of work to be done on that waterway. It is without doubt the greatest tourist resort of any place in Canada. The minister should think of it in terms of tourists rather than in terms of commerce. It is of great importance to Canada to keep these waterways open for tourist traffic, and docks should be built at different places. I do not know whether that would come under the minister's department, but probably he could requisition the public works department to have money spent all along the Trent valley canal at places like Cameron lake, Sturgeon lake, Blossom lake, lake Simcoe, and throughout all that area
Suppl y- Transpo rt

where tourist resorts abound by thousands, and thousands more can be accommodated there if his department does the things it should do.
During the war period I have no doubt that the department was busy with other things, but the war has been over now for three years, and we are looking for developments and for money to be spent along the Trent valley canal which will bring thousands of tourists to Canada, to the benefit of our own economy. If the minister would come up to that part of the country I should be glad to meet him with a boat and give him two weeks holidays in the greatest land of beauty there is in this whole dominion.

I would not want the hon. gentleman to think from any remarks of mine, and I am sure he did not get that impression, that we in the Department of Transport do not give the canal the attention it so well deserves. If my hon. friend will only look at the estimates he will see that we spend a considerable amount of money on the canal each year, and there is also a great deal of revenue coming to the department from the canal. We are spending $347,000 this year on operations and another $84,000 on improvements, which is far more money than is spent on some of the more eastern canals in Ontario. I can assure my hon. friend that we do not intend to neglect the canal, nor have we been neglecting it in any way.
I hope the minister will keep on spending money there for a number of years, because it is required.
We intend to.

I come back to the subject of weeds, in which the minister is not as much interested as I am. Weeds, although humble, have their uses and abuses. The minister has made a distinction that I do not think he will stick to. He has divided navigable streams into two categories; those on which what he called commercial vessels ply, and those on which other kinds of vessels ply. I have here a very large dictionary, and I am going to read a definition of what a navigable river is. It has nothing to do with the kind of ships that ply on it. The definition is: "A river fit to be navigated". These waters we are talking about would be fit to be navigated if the weeds were not allowed to accumulate through the negligence of some government department. I am not sure which department it is, and the question I want to ask the minister is this: Have these weeds in the past been cut by any department?

I understand that they have. Would the minister answer that first? I understand that these weeds have in times past been cut. The obligation to do so was recognized, and it is only of late years that neglect has arisen.

I should perhaps put the position a little more clearly. What I said a moment ago, and if I did not say it I certainly intended to convey that impression, was that there is a doubt in my mind as to the responsibility of the Department of Transport to cut weeds. My hon. friend would like me to make a statement that there is no such responsibility or that there is such responsibility.
I should like to know one way or the other.

I will not say one way or the other. I am making the statement now that there is some doubt in my mind. I do not think I need go any further in explaining the doubt. It is a legal question. That perhaps might have some importance or not; but there is in my mind some doubt, and, that being so, I am sure that the hon. gentleman would not want me to make a statement in so far as the responsibility of the department is concerned which I could not later substantiate.
I want the minister to clear up the doubt now.
I cannot.
Why not?

Because there is doubt in so far as the legal position is concerned. The weeds are there. Do they impede navigation? Do they impede navigation as we understand it in the Department of Transport? I am not familiar with the particular case to which my hon. friend refers and, without knowing the facts, I do not intend to make a statement on it.
I said to the hon. member for Peterborough West a moment ago that, in so far as the particular position was concerned, I would be glad to have it looked into. There are weed cutting apparatuses which can be purchased. I do not know what they cost. Perhaps they are fairly costly. I do not know what the position is. I cannot add anything other than what I have said, namely, that I shall be glad to look at the position from Keene to Rice lake, a channel of some six miles long.
One mile.

I think there are one or two other places.

Sup pi y-Tra nsport
And also Little lake.
There are one or two other places in the vicinity, but I cannot say more than that.

Is the minister to leave us in this position? Is he to tell us that he cannot answer a simple question? He says there is a legal difficulty. What is the Department of Justice for if it cannot solve the difficulty? The minister also used this phrase, "Navigation as we understand it in the Department of Transport." As I understand the minister, he keeps that a closely guarded secret, and he will not tell us what it is. I have not been able to discover what the understanding of navigation is in the Department of Transport. I submit to the minister that it is reasonable for us to ask him to define navigation as it is understood in his department, because this is a matter of considerable substance to the people who live in the tourist areas. It is not academic. I am not hair-splitting. I have had people anxiously consulting me with regard to the same question. We are entitled to an answer on this. Surely the minister is not going to say that there is a legal difficulty. If he does not want to answer the question now, all right; let him answer it tonight or tomorrow or whenever he is prepared to do so. I do not think he should tell us that no answer can be given.

I did not tell the hon. member that no answer can be given. I have given my answer. I am telling him that there is some doubt in my mind as to the responsibility of the Department of Transport to cut weeds. My hon. friend asks what the Department of Justice is for. I suppose I could consult the Department of Justice. I have no objection to doing that; I shall be glad to do it. I cannot give a categorical answer to that.

I am not suggesting that the minister should answer before he is ready. I am only asking him not to leave us in that position.
What is the division of responsibility between public works and transport in this regard? Is there some responsibility on public works?

The responsibility on public works is to build the wharves. Once they are built, we maintain and operate them, except for small expenditures of under $5,000. Public works is responsible for certain dredging, but I do not know that that would include the cutting of weeds, although I cannot speak for my colleague.

The minister mentioned weed-cutting machines. Some years ago the
Department of Transport did look after the weeds. They used to use the old chain method, which is efficient. That has been used for some time on the river at Keene. It used to be used on Chemong lake and was effective, and also in other parts of the Trent canal. The chain method worked very well, and it does not cost very much. They can do a long stretch in a day.
Did I understand the minister to say that the Department of Transport is responsible for docks under S5.000?

I did not put it in that way. I said the Department of Public Works constructs the docks and wharves, and we maintain and operate them; but expenditures on wharves or docks up to $5,000, I understand, are the responsibility of the Department of Transport. My officer corrects me now and tells me that- it is even lower than that. It is expenditure up to $50. There is an item of $5,000-perhaps that is how I got confused-for such repairs up to $50.

Perhaps I can add a word to help the minister arrive at a satisfactory answer to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. The Muskoka river which the hon. member has in mind is at the head of navigation. But not only that; the railway ends there, and the ship which navigates through the lakes is loaded at that point. It delivers all sorts of freight of one kind and another and takes it to various tourist points on the lake. If the weeds are obstructing that channel which is as sinuous as a snake, and it might be possible because of the turns in the river, although the water is otherwise deep enough that weeds would grow as they would do, if they are extending out into the channel, it should not be much of a job to clean them out. The weeds would be an obstruction, not only to a fair-sized boat but also to the power boats. Many power boats come into Bracebridge, load up with material and take it up the lake. I have often boarded a boat there myself for a tour around the lakes. It is an important tourist centre, an important tourist route, and an important tourist lake. If the minister is not familiar with it, perhaps he will take some advisement from me. If he does I am sure he will acquiesce in what my hon. friend asks for. If the weeds are there they should be cut.

If the minister is going to let us know what he considers to be the responsibility in respect of those navigable waters, and also his defini-
Supply-Transport

tion of navigable waters, I am ready to let the matter go on that understanding.
I shall try to get the information on both counts and give it at eight o'clock. I do not know whether I shall be able to get it then, but I shall get it as soon as I can.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
J/77. To provide for breaking ice in Thunder bay, lake Superior and other points deemed advisable in the interests of navigation, $30,000.

I have one matter that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Perhaps we had better leave it until eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock they were considering item 477. But the bon. member for Cumberland wished to speak on item 474 just for a moment.

I wish to thank you, Mr. Chairman, for allowing me to say a few words in connection with aids to navigation under the general heading of marine service. A large amount of money, namely, $3,387,234, is involved. We in Nova Scotia are greatly concerned in these services. We have many lighthouse keepers and these men are the guardians of our shipping. They are on duty day and night the year round in most instances. They perform a necessary and, in many instances, a self-sacrificing service. We have a great deal of sympathy for the mail carriers with respect to their duties and their remuneration. I feel that like consideration is not given to the claims of our lighthouse keepers.
I have in my hand a communication from one of them in my own county. He is Vance F. Barteaux, Cape d'Or, Advocate Harbour, in the western portion of Cumberland county jutting into the bay of Fundy where the tides are high with dense fogs and where there is heavy shipping to both Minas basin and Cumberland basin. This lighthouse keeper has been in the service for twenty-eight years. His station is partly isolated. Although he is on the mainland, be is a distance off the main highway. The roadway which serves this lighthouse is almost completely neglected. I appeal to the minister to have this case looked into, and have the roadway serving this light-

house put into a better state of repair than it is at the present time. The roadway serving the lighthouse is owned by the federal government, while the road leading up to it may be part of the provincial highways. Anyway, it has been neglected and should be placed in better repair.
Then I should like ho make an appeal to the minister, on behalf of this lighthouse keeper and all other lighthouse keepers, that more attention be given to their living quarters. They and their families must live in quarters, which have been more or less neglected. They should have bathrooms and sanitary facilities. They should have electric lights. There Should be an extension of the rural electric services; or if that is not possible, there should be some separate diesel electric systems installed for lighthouses such as these. A rural electric service has been established at Advocate Harbour, within a short distance of this lighthouse. I feel that the lighthouse keeper should have the advantage of this modem facility, and believe that it would be an added advantage for the protection of shipping.
While I am dealing with lighthouses in the province from which I come, I should like, to refer to the range light at Pugwash. That was burned down a number of years ago. At the present time there is just a stick or pole with an electric light. It has a most disgraceful appearance for a structure under the control of the minister's department. I am sure that if the minister saw it he would not tolerate it.
When was it burned down?

I think it was during the war.
I should also like to point out the necessity of improving the channel serving Pugwash harbour. I am pleased that the Minister of Public Works is in his seat at the present time. He will be equally concerned with the Minister of Transport in this matter. The Minister of Transport is responsible for shipping and transport., while the Minister of Public Works will have the responsibility of doing the actual work of widening and improving the shipping channel. I doubt if as much shipping, at as little expenditure of public moneys, has gone through any other harbour in Canada as has gone through Pugwash port, since confederation. In recent years, especially during the war, steamers plying in and out of that port have become larger, and are having more difficulty in navigating the channel. The channel is deep enough, but there are bends where dredging is badly needed. There should also be work done in deepening the outer

Supply-Transport
part of the harbour, at the bar. At the present time the harbour will take a steamer with a 22-foot draft. Ordinarily this is a safe harbour, but the captains and the pilots, who have a great responsibility, should have a better chance to give their ships safe entrance and safe exit. I therefore appeal to the Minister of Transport and to the Minister of Public Works to give this matter special attention. I have spoken to the Minister of Public Works and he has assured me that his department has it under consideration. I hope that some dredging can be done there this year. A large volume of shipping uses Pugwash harbour. This is an expenditure which is well warranted.

I am glad to give my hon. friend the assurance that I will look into the case of the lighthouse keeper to whom he has referred, as well as the condition, of the place in which he lives.
As far as the light at Pugwash is concerned, I have no information as to why it was not rebuilt and ,put back in proper condition. I presume the explanation is that during the war years it may have been found impossible to rebuild it, but I can see no reason why that should not be done. I shall look into the matter and advise my hon. friend.

I wish to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Cumberland, not in reference to any individual case but rather on the general picture as far as the lighthouse keepers on the Atlantic coast are concerned. I have already dealt with the difficulties under which they operate, and I should like to ask the minister whether there has been any reclassification of the salaries of these men. While the minister is saying whether or not there has been any up-grading of salaries, he might also deal with the question of the lighthouse keepers who do not come under the civil service regulations concerning pensions. I refer particularly to the lighthouse keepers in the lower brackets who, after serving for from twenty-five to forty years, are retired without any consideration whatever. On their behalf I make the plea that, instead of these men being retired without any provision for their maintenance, as is the case at present, some method should be devised by means of which they would be given a retiring allowance.

As far as lightkeepers are concerned, I have to tell the hon. gentleman there has been no general reclassification. But
there has been an upward revision in the salaries of most classes of lightkeepers.
Could you give us the salaries?
It is a long document to place on Hansard. Class 1 has been increased from a range of $3,000-83,300 to-
It is those in the lower brackets I am particularly interested in, the men for whom no provision is made. The 83,000 man is entitled to superannuation.

I thought the hon. gentleman was dealing with two questions, first, in connection with the reclassification or upgrading of lightkeepers under the civil service and, second, as to what provision has been made for superannuation of others not under the civil service.
Then give us a couple of classes.
In class 1 there has been an upward revision from a range of 83,00083,300 to a range of S3,480-S3,780.
May I ask how many would be in that class?
I can get that information in a moment.
Not very many, I imagine.

Then let me take class 3. where there has been an upgrading from a range of $2,280-82,580 to a range of 82,580- $2,880. In class 10 the up-grading is from a range of S900-S1,080 to 81,200-81,380; class 11, from a range of $540-8600 to S660-S720; class 12, from $480-8540 to S600-S660. As to the other question concerning those not covered by the civil service, I presume they would be part-time lightkeepers, and there is no provision for superannuation.
Do classes 10, 11 and 12 come under the civil service?
Yes.
The $660 man comes under the civil service?
Yes.

I wonder if I might ask the indulgence of the committee to direct a question to the minister in regard to item 468. We were galloping along so quickly just before the dinner recess that I missed it. I wanted to ask the minister to say a word in general as to whether studies are still proceeding in this connection, or just what we are continuing to do here. I take it that these expenses in connection with the St. Lawrence ship canal have to do with the portion west of Montreal.
Supply-Transport

Last year and again this year an amount has been set aside for the study of the St. Lawrence scheme in general. The explanation I have here is that it is to provide for the continuation of the work now under way in connection with the review of plans and estimates of cost of the various sections of the proposed deep waterway, as well as for the completion of the work now being carried on by the board of engineers for the Lachine section. That is a board which was appointed a short time ago. I thought it was this year, but I am told it was appointed in September of last year. The object in appointing the board was to ascertain whether the scheme of 1926, of the joint board of engineers, is practicable today; to ascertain also whether the scheme could be carried out as a joint navigation and power scheme, and what the cost of a separate navigation scheme would be as compared with a joint power development and navigation scheme; and further to bring the costs up to date and in line with the more recent costs of the international section of the waterway.
Then would the minister answer just one further question. Are the changes which have taken place physical or other changes which might invalidate the previous report?

No, Mr. Chairman. The previous report recommended a navigation scheme only in the Lachine section, but not a power development; whereas in the international section it was a joint scheme. Recently in the international section costs were brought up to date by United States and Canadian engineers, and this board sought to ascertain whether it would be more practicable to have a separate navigation scheme and a separate power scheme, or a joint scheme; and they have not yet reported.

This item has to do with breaking ice in Thunder bay, lake Superior "and other points deemed advisable in the interests of navigation," and in view of that rider which has been tacked on, I want to ask the minister a question. What provision has been made for the keeping of records in connection with the possibility of having navigation into Hudson bay during a greater portion of the year? In discussing this question with the captain of the first ship to enter the strait during the past season, a number of us were told that when he entered the strait there was absolutely no sign of ice either to the naked eye or through the use of radar equipment, that everything was in such condition that he was satisfied he could have entered the strait much

earlier than he did. We also discussed the matter with some of the residents at Churchill, some of whom had lived there prior to the building of the railway. They told us that the mouth of the river was free of ice for a much longer period than that covered by the navigation season. So, if possible, I should like the minister to give us a little resume of any steps the department may be taking to help lengthen that navigation season, which, in view of my information, would seem warranted.

This item provides for the breaking of ice in Thunder bay and is not an expenditure for the Hudson bay area. If my hon. friend wishes to bring that up when we are dealing with the Hudson bay' item, it will be satisfactory.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
480. Life-saving service, including rewards for saving life, $191,285.
Why is there an increase of 8124,915?

The reason for the
increase is the cost of two new lifeboats and the necessary equipment. One is at Bamfield, British Columbia, and the other at Little Wood island, New Brunswick.
Are these both power boats?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
J/81. To provide subsidies for wrecking plants -Quebec and British Columbia, $65,060.
Are those subsidies payable to dry docks?

They are contracts
entered into by the Department of Transport with the Quebec Salvage Company in respect of wrecks on the St. Lawrence, and the Pacific Salvage Company for wrecks on the Pacific coast.
Is that a sort of stand-by fee to have the service available? Is it necessary for the government to subsidize in order to have this service? Cannot the business carry its own load?
It is necessary to subsidize to the extent of entering into a contract. It is a form of insurance.

For many years we had in Nova Scotia a company operating from Halifax, which at one time, if I remember cor-

Supply-Transport
redly, enjoyed a subsidy of $10,000 and, at another time a subsidy of $20,000, while on the Pacific coast the amount was $25,000, and Quebec had a subsidy of $40,000. Why was it necessary to do away with the subsidy paid to the firm in Nova Scotia.

I am afraid I shall have to ask my hon. friend to let me get the information for him. My officers tell me the contract to which he refers is not within their term of office in the department. It must be some years back.

I do not know how long the officers have been with the department, but certainly, since I have been a member of the house, $10,000 was paid at one time to the Maritime Foundation Company. Because of the need for the service, the amount was raised to $20,000. I am not so much concerned about the amount as I am with the service for the Atlantic coast, particularly that portion north of Cape Breton through to Newfoundland. It is a dangerous section and one which should be serviced as carefully as other places in Canada.
I would ask the hon. member to allow me to get the information for him. If I can get it before my estimates are completed, I shall be glad to do so.
I shall be happy to allow the minister to look it up, in the hope that he will consider the request I am placing before him.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
48}. Steamship inspection and the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines, $284,400.
Are these inspectors kept in the same districts all the time, or are they moved from place to place?

Steamship inspection
officials are maintained at points such as Toronto, Montreal, Kingston, Midland and Collingwood, and, when required, they move from those centres to various other regions where steamship inspection is required.

I remember some few years ago a certain steamship was inspected. Not long after the inspection, I went aboard and I would not have put a dog in one of their lifeboats. They were not safe. The man who did the inspection is dead. I wonder if a proper check is made?
I cannot comment on the particular case to which my hon. friend is referring.
I understand that.

If in the hon. member's estimation there was a breach of regulation I should be glad to look into the matter. I do not know the details. However, the inspection branch of the department have regulations under which they operate, and by which they must abide. They must see that a ship is not given a certificate or allowed to sail unless it has the required equipment and is in seaworthy condition.
Are these inspectors wholly employed by the government?
Yes.
They are not allowed to do other work?
No.
Some inspections used to be made by men who were known as inspectors, but who at the same time had other occupations.
Not since I have been in the department.
No; that was some time ago.
Probably so; I am not able to answer the question.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
486. River St. Lawrence ship channel-contract dredging in the St. Lawrence river and Montreal harbour, including cost of administration

capital, $3,492,000.
What is the explanation of the large increase for contract dredging?

This is a contract which provides for the dredging of the St. Lawrence river from Montreal harbour to some forty miles below Quebec. The item appears by virtue of a contract which has been entered into, the provisions of which cover the widening of the channel to a certain width. It varies from 550 feet to, in some places, 1,500 feet, on the curve, and to a depth of thirty-five feet. The contract was entered into, providing for the expenditure of a certain amount of money over the years.
The reason for the increase is that it is expected for this year it will be possible to spend more money than last year, on account
Supply-Transport

of the fact that last year the company was late in getting started. The engineers of the ship channel feel that it would be possible for the company to do this amount of work in the coming season.
This is a contract which is let out?
Yes.
How much of it is administrative, and what is the significance of the expression "including cost of administration", when the contract is let out?
I do not think any of it is administration.
It says so.
It is by contract price.

Perhaps the minister will read it. It states:
River St. Lawrence ship channel; contract dredging in the St. Lawrence river and Montreal harbour, including cost of administration.
Is this all the dredging that is proposed to be done this year on the St. Lawrence?

Yes. I am afraid I shall have to ask my hon. friend to allow his question to stand, and I will get the answer is quickly as possible.
Item stands.
Marine service-
487. River St. Lawrence ship channel-administration, operation and maintenance, $495,278.

The same question of administration arises. I am particularly interested because this is another item covering the river St. Lawrence ship channel, administration, while item 486 also includes the cost of administration. How much of item 486 is administration?

The St. Lawrence ship channel administration has its head office in Montreal. There is an engineer in charge with a staff, and his business is to supervise the dredging in the St. Lawrence. Will the minister tell us briefly the functions of the Canadian maritime commission and how long it has been in existence?

The maritime commission was set up only recently, in November or December of 1947. Since its establishment, the commission has had many duties to perform. It has made recommendations to the government on many problems faced by Canadian shipping and shipbuilding industries. Its main problem has been that of modernizing the Canadian fleet to enable Canadian ship owners to meet foreign competition more effectively.
The Canadian fleet now consists of the war-built ex-Park ships, sold by the government to private Canadian shipping companies on liberal terms, with a restrictive flag transfer clause prohibiting their being resold with transfer of registry. Many ship owners now require faster, newer and more specialized ships for their services, and the commission is carrying out a tonnage replacement plan which makes it possible for Canadian ship owners who need new tonnage to sell their ex-Park ships to foreign purchasers, on condition that the Canadian owners discharge their mortgages before sale and deposit the sale proceeds in escrow for the building of new ships in Canada. Up to the present time, eight ships have been sold under this plan.
Another duty of the commission is to inquire into and report upon practical problems affecting Canadian shipping which may be referred to it from time to time by the government.
For example?

For example, it has investigated and made recommendations upon the carrying of cargoes under ERP in Canadian bottoms. Another of its duties and responsibilities was to review the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act.

Supply-Transport
In carrying out its work the commission has had to confer with other departments from time to time. There is what is known as the knock-for-knock agreement between Canada and the United States, which during the war years was administered by and under the jurisdiction of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Those duties are now transferred to the maritime commission. It has further undertaken the control and direction of two government agencies dealing with shipping matters; that is, the steamship subsidies branch, which is more particularly dealt with in the estimates and which was formerly a part of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and Park Steamships.

We on the extreme east coast were very much interested in the creation of this maritime commission, and I think that applies equally to those on the west coast. We were hopeful that a long-range program would be drawn up and made public with respect, to the duties of this commission.

To set up such a system, I believe it is necessary to have, not men who come from one particular section of Canada but men who will represent the whole of this country, men who are familiar with both east and west coasts as well as the ports of Montreal and Quebec. I have nothing to say against Quebec or Montreal in regard to their shipping facilities; but, speaking more particularly for the east coast at the moment, I say we are aiming for greater export trade and greater shipping activity.
To repeat what I have frequently said on the floor of this house, during the war period Canada made great use of the eastern ports. They were busy spots, with ships going in and out. We had ships sailing even- four minutes to make up convoys totalling from sixty to one hundred vessels. So it was very busy at Halifax, Saint John and the other ports. Today there is not the same activity. When the maritime commission was set up we hoped it would inaugurate some program which would bring back those prosperous times as far as our ports were concerned.

the gentlemen who compose it, but I am advised that the chairman is a lawyer, no doubt a man of ability and outstanding in his own profession but with no practical experience as far as shipping is concerned on either coast. Perhaps I should follow my hon. friend's suggestion and enlarge somewhat upon the statement I made a moment ago concerning the maritime commission. Canada's wartime shipbuilding program produced 441 cargo ships totalling approximately 3,810,000 deadweight tons. These vessels were all built in Canadian yards by Canadian labour. I need not dilate upon the value of the service which these vessels rendered during the strenuous war years, because my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce has already dealt with that at some length in a statement he made in the house on June 16, 1947, which can be found at page 4195 of Hansard.
I might remind the committee, however, that the Park fleet, which was composed of 176 vessels, cost the government the sum of approximately $277,500,000; and in spite of the
