fact that they were regarded in the same light as munitions of war, nevertheless the government succeeded in recovering the sum of approximately 8199,500,000, being seventy-two per cent of their original cost, through the operation of these ships and their sale to private operators after the end of the war.
In order to maintain a Canadian flag fleet, the government has sold practically the entire fleet to Canadian operators, including seventy-eight vessels still on charter to the British ministry of transport, which vessels are now in process of being returned to Canada. One of the conditions of sale was that no owner is permitted to apply for transfer out of Canadian registry without permission of the Canadian government.
After making preliminary studies, the Canadian maritime commission has advised me that the restriction against transfer of flag is leaving the Canadian fleet in a static condition. While the vessels built for war purposes are suitable in some trade as bulk carriers, they are not competitive with new tonnage which has been and is being built in other countries. If the Canadian flag is to continue on the high seas, it must be maintained by a well-balanced fleet consisting not only of bulk carriers but of faster and more modern units with refrigerator capacity able to compete with vessels of other flags on scheduled services.
The Canadian shipping industry is in its infancy. Prior to the war, Canada did not have a fleet of ocean-going dry cargo vessels. While there is no doubt that government policy has stimulated the shipping and shipbuilding industry, there is no doubt that the Canadian shipowners must be afforded at least an opportunity of selling vessels which are becoming obsolescent, in order to acquire efficient units.
To enable Canadian owners to acquire such vessels to modernize their fleets, the government, on the recommendation of the Canadian maritime commission, has now adopted a policy of. permitting sales of ex-Park vessels for' transfer, to foreign registry. Any owner desiring to sell must apply to the maritime commission for permission to do so. The commission investigates the circumstances fully and determines whether or not the sale of an ex-Park vessel and replacement by modern tonnage will be to the advantage of Canadian trade.
In so doing, it * takes into consideration in particular the competition with which the vessel is faced in the specific trade in which it is engaged. If the commission decides that it is advantageous to secure replacement, the owner is given permission to sell to any pur-

chaser approved by the commission, subject also to the approval of the commission as to price and terms of sale.
The owner is required to discharge fully any indebtedness due to the government in respect of the purchase of the vessel from the government, and then must deposit the proceeds of sale in escrow with the commission to secure replacement by modern tonnage. The commission reserves the right to approve the plans of the new ship and the terms and conditions for her construction, and the new ship must be maintained under Canadian registry.
It is anticipated that ships built under this scheme will be constructed in Canadian yards, provided that costs of Canadian shipbuilders are kept within reason, and if not, the commission may, under special circumstances, allow owners to acquire tonnage abroad. It is not expected, however, that this will be the case, and it is hoped that the escrow fund will provide a backlog for shipbuilding in Canada for some years to come.
A number of rumours have recently been circulated to the effect that Canada's fleet is being put on the auction block or that transfers are being permitted to enable Canadian owners to take advantage of low-cost labour in foreign countries. This is definitely not the case.
There will be no great volume of sale in the near future, and modernization of the Canadian fleet will be a matter of gradual development. The original Park fleet being built for war purposes, the accommodation for seamen in some cases leaves much to be desired, and there is no question that the building of modern tonnage will improve the living conditions for all seamen. The replacement policy will afford employment for Canadian shipyard labour, and the new vessels to be constructed will not only further Canada's overseas trade but be a credit to the Canadian flag.
The senior hon. member for Halifax referred to subventions being administered by the department. I have a lengthy statement on not only that, but other activities of the commission. I gave my statement briefly in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, when he referred to the personnel of the commission.
Of course, when one is setting up a new body such as this it is almost impossible to have on it representatives of all interested groups in the country, those interested in shipbuilding, seamen, operators, exporters, and importers on the great lakes, and the like.

Supply-Transport
In order to do that, we would have to have a body of perhaps seven or eight. The government came to the conclusion, however, that a commission composed of three members would answer the purpose.
The chairman of that commission, Mr. Clyne, is a man of wide experience, experience which he has obtained on the west coast. He has been handling maritime matters, legally and otherwise, for the greater part of his adult life, and he is well equipped to fulfil all these duties.
What is his profession?
He is a lawyer.
A lawyer?
Yes. The other member of the commission was in the Department of of External Affairs for some years. He was an officer in the navy during the war, with a distinguished career.
Who is the third one? There are three members?
Yes.
The chairman and two commissioners?
Yes.
Who is the third one?
The third one is Mr. Rahlves, who was president and manager of-
"Is" or "was"?
"Was." I was going to say in a minute that he had resigned. He was general manager of Park Steamships during the war and had a wide experience in the operation of ships.
The minister did not tell us where the second member resided or lived.
The second member lives in Ottawa.
Ottawa?
Yes.
One from the west coast and one from Ottawa; is that right?
One from the west coast and one from the central part of Canada.
Now hon. members will appreciate the point I am trying to get at, that we should have one from the eastern maritime provinces, as a third member.

I wish to support the senior member for Halifax. I thought, 5849-316i
when this commission was first set up, it would operate in place of what was known as the maritime rights commission for the benefit of the maritimes. There is no part of Canada more interested in maritime matters to which this commission would give attention than are the maritime provinces. I agree wholeheartedly with the senior member for Halifax when he says that one of the members of the commission should come from the maritime provinces.
While I do not want to be too definite about it, I still have doubts about the necessity for this commission. The Department of Transport is well officered. I think it should be able to administer the duties placed in the hands of this commission to at least as good satisfaction as would the commission, at great saving in costs. I have great respect for the officials in the minister's department, and most of the higher officers in the civil service. I am under the impression that they could carry on the duties assigned to this commission at a great saving to the taxpayers and with at least as great, if not greater, efficiency.
What was the exact reason for setting up this commission in 1947? Had some other organization disappeared and was there a gap that had to be filled?

It did not replace any other organization; it was a new body that had been requested during the war years by various groups in Canada. When the matter was debated in the house there were many strong supporters on my hon. friend's side, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver South.
All parts of the house.

That is as it may be, but I do not remember. The minister says this did not take the place of any body that had existed before. As far as I could make out from what he said, there was no new work that they had to take up. As far as I could follow what he said, it would seem to me that the work must have greatly decreased since the war years and the immediately subsequent time.
However that may be, I want to associate myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Cumberland. After listening to what the minister has said as to the duties, I cannot for the life of me understand Why the people in his department could not carry them out. It seems to me that this 19 just another of these commissions set up for the purpose of spoon-feeding people and holding the hands
Supply-Transport

of people whose hands do not need to be held. I notice that they have bo approve contracts, investigate this and give judgment on that. I do not know whether they are competent to do so, because I do not know the gentlemen; I am not offering any opinion on that, but when I look at this item of $134,000 I wonder whether it is going to make a single extra dollar for the people of Canada. I would gravely doubt it.
When I look on this building of commission on commission it seems to me that we have a mania for this kind of thing. I was astounded at a figure given the other day, I believe by the Winnipeg Free Press. However, upon reflection I am afraid that it must be true. They stated that the various taxing bodies in this country are taking something like one-third of our national income. They went on to state, and I think it was fairly stated, that that is higher than in any other country in the world. I am quoting those figures subject to correction, but I believe they were put forward by competent people and are absolutely true. Again may I say that I doubt very much if in his heart the minister will disagree with the statement that the $134.400-
I disagree most heartily.

The minister can speak for himself. Nothing that the minister has said tonight makes me feel that this $134,000 will add a single dollar to the wealth of this country or that the services which are being performed can not be performed by the perfectly competent people in his department. We have a list here, as long as your arm, of engineers and competent people of various kinds. I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce wishes to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
In addition to carrying out duties that were not performed before, this commission is taking over the duties of the Park Steamship Company, which at the height of its career operated some 200 Ships for the government. The commission is carrying on functions which were held over from the Park Steamship Company. It is operating boats that are only partly paid for, and it is discharging functions that were formerly carried on by the Department of Trade and Commerce, namely, those having to do with steamship subsidies.
It seems to me that this commission has onerous and continuous duties. I suggest that, if anything, it is under-staffed rather than over-staffed.
I understand that Park Steamship Company is now being operated by private interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
Whom is it being operated by?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: By the maritime commission. The Park Steamship Company is a crown company. Some of the ships which were formerly operated privately through the Park Steamship Company have been sold, but there are continuing functions of the Park Steamship Company still being carried on.
Did it not have an adequate staff to run its affairs? Was it not carrying on before 1937?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is no Park Steamship Company today, but the duties are being carried on by the commission.
I do not understand the minister. He says in one breath that the duties are being carried on by the commission, and in the next breath he says the ships are being operated by a crown company.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The crown company has been disbanded.

May I add just a word? The hon. member for Cumberland has suggested that there is no function for this organization. There is a similar organization in the 'United Kingdom and in the United States. The object of the commission is to protect shipping for the country. If we were to follow the same steps we followed during the last war we would lose all our ships. The commission is to interest itself in a shipping program for Canada. By the amalgamation of the operations of the Park Steamship Company with those of the maritime commission, there has been a saving of $80,000 a year.
I want to commend the minister most highly for his endeavours to build up a shipping fleet in this country and to maintain it at something like efficiency.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Could the minister provide a little information on some of the aspects of the operations of this commission? I understood from what has been said tonight that it is largely concerned with ocean-going steamers of 10,000 tons or thereabouts, but recently it has embraced in its scope fishing boats and fishing schooners. An advisory committee has been set up to advise on small boats and sailing vessels.
Another commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
So far as I know, there is nobody with any practical experience or knowledge of fishing boats on this commission.

Supply-Transport
My attention was directed to that point by the remarks of the senior member for Halifax who asked that someone with practical experience in maritime matters generally be placed on the commission. I receive letters almost daily from people in the fishing industry who ask what the Canadian maritime commission intends to do about the fishing industry and in what respect their boats come under the commission. I have also had letters asking me to indicate who with any knowledge of fishing boats will be on the commission. To date I have not been able to find out very much about this, and I should like the minister to make a statement.
There is another uncertainty creeping into this picture. In the Halifax press and, I presume, in the press across the country, there was a story that three ocean-going transports were being tied up at Halifax because they could not compete with ships of other nations. Then, on the strength of the announcement made by the minister that our merchant ships are being sold, the presumption grows that they will be sold to competing nations who can operate them with mariners at lower rates of pay, and thus put us in an unfavourable position. The sale of our ships is likely to aggravate the situation and also the status of fishing boats, in the harbour at Halifax. I wish the minister would take a minute or two to clarify that situation and also the status of fishing boats.

There are several matters which the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has brought up. First, he asked whether the operations of the maritime commission cover only foreign-going vessels. The answer is generally yes: but it also has to do with other duties such as I outlined in the statement I made when we took up this item, such as subsidies for coastal vessels, the administration of steamship subventions, and generally advising the government on policy.
The hon. gentleman asks if there is anyone with experience or knowledge of the fishing boat industry. The answer is no, there is not, because that is not directly a responsibility of the commission. However, under the Maritime Commission Act provision is made to set up advisory committees, and one of the advisory committees that has been set up in case it may be necessary for the government to seek advice is represented by the fisheries council.
My hon. friend feared that these vessels which were sold might compete with our own vessels. That is what we are trying to avoid by setting up the policy of the transfer of flag in certain cases. It is to bring our ships up to the highest possible standard, to streamline and modernize our fleet, so that competition will not overtake us. We are beginning to notice that other countries are building bigger, faster and more modern ships than our Park vessels. In order to compete we have to do likewise, and we have accordingly adopted the policy set out in the memorandum I read a moment ago. The policy was adopted just to obviate and counteract the situation to which my hon. friend referred.

Would the minister be good enough to answer these questions? How many ships were operated by the Park Steamship Company during the war; how many ships were sold, and how many are being operated at the present time?

The following ships were sold to Canadian companies for operation under the Canadian flag: one hundred and fifteen 10,000-ton ships; twenty-two 4,700-ton ships, or a total of 137.
The following Canadian-owned ships are still on charter to the United Kingdom ministry of transport: twenty 10,000-ton ships. They are being returned from the United Kingdom to Canada in 1948 for delivery to Canadian purchasers; also, fifty-eight 10.000-ton ships, which will remain on charter to the United Kingdom ministry until 1950, when they also will be returned for delivery to Canadian purchasers.
The United Kingdom ministry will retain for an indefinite period seven 10,000-ton "stores issuing" ships and eight 10,000-ton "maintenance" ships.
Canada's fleet of ocean-going ships of over 500 gross tons therefore consists of 229 dry cargo ships, with a total deadweight capacity of approximately 2,100,000 tons.
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario); Who operates those?

These are ex-Park vessels which have been sold to private operators. Some of them have been sold on terms and have been chartered. Those that have been chartered are still being administered by the maritime commission in its capacity of successor to Park Steamships.
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoha-Ontario) r What does the minister mean by administered? Operated?

No. Park Steamships
is out of operation altogether. I mean collecting charter hire.

Do you need a commission costing 8134,000 to collect charter hire?
Supply-Transport
No, my hon. friend did not understand me, or perhaps I did not make myself clear. I do not want to be offensive at all.
I think we- shall get on better now that your . colleague is away.

The duties of the maritime commission with reference to Park Steamships are only a very small portion of its functions because Park Steamships is being gradually, if not entirely, wound up. It did operate these ships during wartime and they are gradually being sold. The commission has taken over those that remain and will soon wind up the operations of Park Steamships.
That is grand. You have torpedoed what your colleague said and now we are getting the facts.

I have tried not to be offensive, but if my hon. friend wants to take my colleague to task in that manner I am afraid he and I will not get along. I do not think it is fair for my hon. friend to say that I have torpedoed what my colleague said or that he has torpedoed what I said. I am tiying to be helpful.
I think you are.
I am doing the best I can, but if my hon. friend wants to be critical-
I am not being critical of you.

-I am quite prepared to put up with it. If my hon. friend wants to know what the duties of the commission are I have already put them on the record once and have explained them twice. The duties of the commission are of an advisory nature. I am positive that the commission is doing a very fine job. The House of Commons approved the work of the commission when it passed the bill last year. The bill was debated at great length, and was supported, if my recollection serves me aright, by all parts of the house and by many hon. members from that side of the house. It was then conceded that it was necessary, in fact urgent, to have the maritime commission established. Many members from my hon. friend's side of the house had been continually advocating the formation of the commission long before action was taken and, indeed,

took rny colleague the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to task for not having moved earlier. So I do not think it is a nullity in the department. I think the commission is very necessary and is performing a good service, without which we could not have a shipping industry to compete with those of other countries.

I started this question. It was a fairly simple question, and I think the minister can answer it one, two, three. How many ships were operated-I am not talking about their size or anything else

during the war by the -Park Steamship Company? How many ships have since been sold; how many are at present being operated and come under the direct control of the maritime commission? These are three simple questions.

The answer to the first question, how many ships were operated by Park, is 238 approximately. The answer to the second question, how many were sold, the same number. The answer to the third question, how many operated under the commission, none, except for the purpose of completing the charter hire and collecting the money under the charter hire.
Now we have the answer. No ships are being operated by the maritime commission. What are their duties?

I want to thank the minister for getting us part of the way on. AVe have now got rid of the idea of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this is an operating unit. The minister has made it clear that, so far as operating Park Steamships is concerned, what it does is receive payments. It does not need a 8134,000 commission to do that.
The minister has said, and on this I should like further information, that the commission advises and is apparently to keep up the level of our shipping, is to consider our foreign trade and the kind of ships we should have. It seems to me that on that we are entitled to a little further information. I am still skeptical. I still do not see why it is that when you establish a business someone should come along and tell you what to do. I am glad to see that the senior hon. member for Halifax is with me. I would like to know if the minister can go a little more fully into what the functions of these gentlemen are. So far as I am concerned, I am completely in the dark. If I may add something. I am carrying it in my mind that the minister has competent, scientific, expert advisers, who, with all due deference to the profession with which I had once

Supply-Transport
a bowing acquaintance, seem more competent to advise him on these technical questions than a lawyer.

I have already said what the commission's work was since its establishment. Perhaps I can summarize it again. The main problem that the commission has to deal with is, as I said a moment ago, that of modernizing the Canadian fleet to enable Canadian shipowners to meet foreign competition more effectively.
Will the minister permit a question there?

Will my hon. friend allow me to answer his question? This means that Canadian ship operators have to meet keen competition because new, more modern and faster ships are being put onto certain trade routes, so that our ship operators who are doing business with ex-Park vessels, that is 10,000-ton freighters, 4,700-ton freighters and certain tankers, find themselves at a disadvantage. Therefore the commission has adopted a program whereby it will allow some of these operators to sell their Park vessels, but not to sell them unless the purchase price is deposited in escrow, and the money used for the purchase of new ships, of the type necessary to compete on the trade routes, to be built in Canadian shipyards. That in itself is a man-sized job.
Then, as I said a moment ago, the commission has inquired into and reported upon several practical problems. One of them I gave to the hon. gentleman. It has investigated and made recommendations upon the question of the role of Canadian shipping in the European recovery program. The Canada Shipping Act, which was amended and passed in this house, was given attention by the commission. As a central agency, another of the duties of the commission is the administration of shipping matters. The commission has given assistance to Canadian ship owners in many fields. The commission has a responsibility for investigation, certification and settlement of claims in the knock-for-knock agreement. It has undertaken the control and direction of two government agencies, steamship subsidies and the remainder of the activities of Park Steamships.
The commission has not yet been in existence for a year, and it still has other duties to perform. The future commission expects it will take about six months to complete a survey of the shipbuilding industry. In carrying out this survey, the commission will obtain and consider the recommendations of ship owners, ship builders, labour organizations, exporters, importers, manufacturers, primary producers
and other Canadian interests and other organizations affected by shipping policy. That was the object of appointing the advisory committees authorized under the act. I do not know that I can give the hon. gentleman any more complete details than that.

I am not going to pursue the matter further. I just want to say this, without wishing to be in the least offensive to the minister. I think what he said was just a lot of words. I would be much happier to have the minister make these decisions himself, along with some expert person with whom he might consult from day to day. I would far rather rely on that than this commission which is spending tens of thousands of dollars on things which, to me, are just a lot of-I do not want to use extreme words. I think the whole thing is unreal.

I want to support this item of $134,000 for the administration of the Canadian maritime commission. I supported the resolution which preceded the bill and I still support it. I have some knowledge of marine matters. I fully realize that if we do not have the maritime commission, or some equivalent body, our merchant marine will go down to what it was before. At that time it was practically negligible. Canada had one of the largest merchant fleets in the world in the old sailing ship days when Nova Scotia, Quebec, New Brunswick and the maritime provinces generally owned so many ships. They dwindled down to practically nothing.
This maritime commission is in its infancy. Hon. members can criticize it now and criticize it justly. I think the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has brought out some pertinent points. The commission has to be broadened in its scope. It has to get more men with practical knowledge of marine matters than it has at the present time. The commission is just growing up. I support the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and also the senior hon. member for Halifax. I think they brought out some useful points, but we must have this commission.
The company with which I was concerned prior to going into the army in 1939 imported from the old country. Most of our cargoes came in Scandinavian bottoms. The reason was that our Canadian ships and the British ships could not compete with the Scandinavians. The maritime commission may be able to help out in that regard. If we are to have a merchant fleet we may have to subsidize under certain circumstances, but we must have a body of specialists who can handle this. The Department of Transport as such
Supply- Tran sport

cannot do it. I am quite positive of that. They must have an advisory body. I do recommend that more men with practical marine experience be brought in and that the scope of the commission be broadened. I particularly want to see the fishing vessels and the smaller craft brought in here. I think we would be making a great mistake if we did not support this item. This body is just in its infancy, and in the years to come hon. members will realize that they have been wise in having established a maritime commission.

It is not a case of supporting the item; it is a case of trying to find out something about it. What is meant by "Professional and special services, $25,000''? No amount was voted for this item last year, but we are asked for $25,000 this year.
It is provision for audits in connection with steamship subventions.
That is right.
How much do they audit?
Let me take a minute to explain this to my hon. friend.
I wish you would.

There has been a demand for increased subventions. That demand is because of increased costs; and the government has felt that before increases were granted, there should be an accounting of the books of certain of the applicants. That is a sensible thing to do. Before you pay out money, it is logical to ascertain whether those who claim that conditions require increased subsidies, are correct in their statement, and whether their figures can be verified. An audit has been made in a number of cases, and this item is for that purpose.
These are subsidies that are paid out from the minister's department?
That is right.
These are subsidies for mail, mostly, are they not?
Yes; the items following, in votes 495 and 496.
Just following this up, does the treasury department not make audits of this?
I did not catch the question.
Does the minister's own department not make audits of this?

We have, no auditors in the Department of Transport. There is in fact an auditor or two in the board of transport- commissioners, but their work has to do with railway matters. There is no auditor in the Department of Transport.
You mean to say that subsidies are given without any check-up on them?
Oh, oh.
That is what it looks like.
That is exactly what it is not; and that is exactly what I am telling my hon. friend this provision is for.
The minister stated that this has been set up for only about a year.
No, I did not say that.
The minister said that this commission had been set up for only about a year.

But not steamships
subventions. Those have been in existence for years.
Yes; but evidently there was no audit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon.
member for Grey North.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The port of Owen Sound.

The minister says there has been an application for an increase in subventions. As I review the details of the services at page 276 of the estimates, it would certainly appear that there has been a tremendous demand for an increase in salaries. Just let me review this matter to some extent. For the chairman of the commission there is an increase from $5,000 to $12,000.
For part of a year.

Yes. There are two commissioners at $20,000 a year. Why could not the scope of their administration be enlarged? From listening to the discussion and the answers given by the minister, I cannot understand how these men are fully employed in the task which he has outlined, because it would appear that their responsibilities are less. I am thinking now that a maritime or marine commission could administer the affairs on the great lakes in which I am particularly interested. The. city of Owen Sound has, I think I can say without fear of contradiction, one of the finest harbours on the great lakes. It is the last to freeze up in the fall and the first to open in the spring. That

Supply-Transport
can be verified. For years the board of trade and other public bodies have appealed to the Minister of Transport to allow the lightship St. Heliers to be in the port of Owen Sound. The mariners have also appealed, because markers are put out early in the spring and then in the fall. We have not been able to get anywhere with that suggestion. I have had an opportunity to review some of the correspondence between, the minister and the board of trade and between the board of trade and the minister, and I cannot for the life of me understand why, when you are putting lightships there, those ships should be wintered in Midland.
We are past that item.

I am speaking of the advisability of enlarging the duties of the commission, so that the minister's estimate of $134,300 might be more properly justified. I rose a while ago to discuss this item and I was told I was wrong. I may be wrong now. I should be glad if the minister could tell me now why the present procedure is necessary, and why we have not the advantage of one of these lightships placing markers for the benefit of mariners for life-saving and so on. It means a great deal to them as they ply the great lakes and the boats go down from the head of lake Superior, from Port Arthur and Fort William, with their cargoes late in the fall and leave the port early in the spring. If it would not be asking too much, I should like to have the minister say why we have not one of these ships in the port of Owen Sound.

The hon. member is not asking for too much. I can tell him that the maritime commission has absolutely no jurisdiction over the subject which he raised a moment ago. The St. Heliers lightship is a matter that comes under marine sendees. I know the position fairly well. I had representations from my hon. friend. It is certainly not a matter over which the maritime commission would have any jurisdiction.

I wish to support the remarks made by the senior member for Halifax, which were to the effect that when appointment is made of a successor to Mr. Rahlves on the Canadian maritime commission, consideration be given to appointing a man from the maritime provinces. I have the utmost respect for the chairman of the commission, Mr. dyne, and his associate, Captain Audette. I think they are both competent and capable men. But in matters pertaining to the east coast, I submit that we should have a man of experience in matters pertaining to that coast. This is more particularly true, because 5849-317
a large number of the ships owned and operated by Park Steamships was sold to Atlantic Shippers with head office in Halifax. At the moment three of their ships are tied up in the port of Halifax. For these reasons I submit that great attention should be paid to the remarks made by the senior member for Halifax, and that every avenue should be canvassed in trying to get a suitable man from the maritimes to take the place of Mr. Rahlves.
I can assure my hon. friend! that every consideration has been and is being given to that matter.

Item agreed to.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions-
49-4. Administration, $19,949.

I should like to bring before the committee and the minister the matter of the subsidy on a service across Minas basin. This was for a ferry service which was established forty-five or fifty years ago to serve the people in Annapolis valley and Cumberland, and, in more recent years, to serve the tourists. In about the year 1926 a special boat was built to operate on that service. It was called the Kipawo, a name which is formed from the first two letters of the ports at which it called, namely Kingsport, Parrsboro and Wolfville: Kingsport in Kings county, Parrsboro in Cumberland county and Wolfville in Kings county. We made the sacrifice of allowing that ferry boat, which carried cars, to be taken over by the naval department about 1942, with the expectation that it would be restored to the service. This was one service that was subsidized by the federal government and by the provincial government. I think the federal government gave $4,500 or $5,000 a year and the provincial government the same amount. That boat was taken over by the naval service and finally transferred to Newfoundland. At the end of the war it was sold by war assets for $26,000, fully as much as was paid for it in the first place; it was not a large boat.
The people of that section of Nova Scotia were much annoyed and put out by the action of the department in not restoring this boat and this subsidy. The provincial government supported it and offered to pay its portion as before. It made representations to the federal government. At that time shipping subsidies were under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I believe the then minister was sympathetic; because it rvas the only subsidy in all Canada that was discontinued, notwithstanding the fact that this ferry service had been in operation for more than
Supply-Transport

forty years. Boards of trade in the maritime provinces and interested people made repeated representations. Hundreds of boats were acquired by the government in the naval service and the Park Steamship Company, mentioned by the minister, but not one was made available to renew this ferry service.
During the war, motorists had to go 150 miles further. Gasoline wyas scarce; it was almost impossible to get tires, but our people made the sacrifice and were willing to continue to make it as long as necessary, as Nova Scotians did in every phase of the war effort. But they did expect this service to be re-established at the end of the war; they did expect this boat to be brought back, but it was sold and the proceeds held by the federal government.
I request the minister to look into this grievance and have the service restored. It is only about nine miles from Parrsboro to Kingsport, and about fifteen miles to Wolf-ville. An improvement might be made by having direct connection from Parrsboro to Blomidon, the nearest point in King's county, which is only three and a half miles away. If a wharf were built there it would be only a short service from Parrsboro across the Minas basin. It would land at a point on Blomidon, which is being advocated by the government of Nova Scotia and by many people as the site of a national park.
Now that the subsidies come under the minister's direction, I would ask him to deal with this matter. I do not believe the people in any other part of Canada would have been subjected to this treatment. We in Nova Scotia are long suffering or we would not have put up with it. This was the only subsidy discontinued in all Canada, just because we sacrificed our boat in order to be of service during the war. I believe this ferry should be re-established as a service to the local people, as a service to tourists, and as a matter of pride for the whole countryside. The destruction of this service is another sign of retrogression, and the people concerned are very much grieved and hurt. I ask the minister to give this matter his personal attention.
I should like to speak on this general item-
I wonder if I can get a statement from the minister concerning this matter.

My bon. friend has raised two points; the service between Blomidon and Parrsboro and between Parrsboro and Hantsport and Windsor. The position

is as he stated, that the service was taken off during the war; but, as I understand the duties of the steamship subventions branch of the commission, they do not include establishing a service, but rather deciding whether or not a subsid3? is necessary for the operation of a service.
But in this case-

Would the hon. gentleman permit me to continue? If someone makes an application to operate a ferry service between these points, unquestionably the commission will have to give the matter its attention, I would even go a step further and say the commission can and will look into it and, after doing so, they may decide to intervene. But it is not the business of the commission to institute service. It may be that some injustice is being done to the citizens of these points, but that is not a matter with which the commission is directly charged. I take it that there is no service between Blomidon and Parrsboro, and my information is that there is no wharf at Blomidon, so that I suppose there would be some considerable expenditure before such a service could be considered, since a wharf would have to be built. I do not want my hon. friend to think we are not prepared to give the subject he has raised every consideration. I shall ask the commission to look into it and see if something can be done to assist the people in that area.

I want to thank the minister for going as far as he did, but I point out to him and to this committee that we are not asking the government to establish a newT service. The government destroyed the service which was there for forty or fifty years, so that they have a very real responsibility to see that the service is re-established. They took the boat which was specially built under the authority of the province of Nova Scotia when I was provincial minister of highways, and which operated there from 1926 or 1927 until 1942. That boat was taken over by the naval department and sold by war assets; and we have been denied that, service ever since.

I should like to speak on this general item. The hon. member for Cumberland has just said the people of Nova Scotia are long suffering and hard done by. The senior hon. member for Halifax was complaining that, because of the lack of a maritime provinces man, on the maritime commission he thought, the people of the mari-times were not getting as fair a break as other

Supply-Transport
parts of Canada. But looking at pages 72 and 73 of the estimates, I would suggest that the maritimes are doing extremely well, as far as .mail subventions are concerned. For the west coast of British Columbia we have three items totalling some $79,000. For the maritimes we have a page and a half of items totalling about $1,150,000.
As I pointed out a little earlier this session, during the debate on the Canada Shipping Act, coastal shipping on the British Columbia coast is of much greater significance than that on the east coast, because of our total lack of north and south roads. A tremendous volume of traffic moves up and down the coast. There is a small subsidy for the service on the west coast of Vancouver island and a small subsidy for service between Prince Rupert and the Queen Charlotte islands, but my point is that there has been a very great difference between the subsidies paid on the west coast and those on the east coast.
My second point is that, since the end of the war, a condition has arisen which makes the need for these subsidies on the west coast very much greater. Before the war, we had three services on the west coast: the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and a small coastal line known as Union Steamships, which called at all the small ports. It was a slow service but a good service, in that no logging camp or fishing village was too small for Union Steamships to push in, drop off the mail and push on. After the war, quite a number of naval veterans thought they should enter this coastal trade. They bought some of these war vessels, which apparently the department thought very little of, but which these people thought a great deal of. Then they reconverted them. In my riding alone there are four of these coastal lines. These lines decided to service only the bigger points of Gibsons Landing, Sechelt, Pender Harbour, Powell River and Britannia Mine. They picked the cream of the trade, leaving the Union Steamships calling at the smaller points, in which they have mail contracts, thus losing the business out of the big points.
As a consequence, the only thing the bigger company could do was to begin to drop their service to the smaller points. I am sure the maritime commission will know the points I am referring to-Halfmoon bay, Lang bay, Lund and Egmont. These little points are all along the coast. Their only connection with Vancouver is by sea. There is no road and no rail connection. No subsidy is paid to this new line, and certainly insufficient subsidy to the Union Steamships to justify that service. So they have dropped the service.
The unfortunate member of parliament for that district, the hon. member for Vancouver North, gets the full complaint: "Why is this happening?" Most abuse is against the steamship company, the residents not realizing the situation which the company has to face.
For the entire mainland coast of British Columbia, from Vancouver to Stewart, which is about GOO miles direct and about 5,000 miles by coast line, we have a subsidy of $37,000 which, I suppose, is divided among the three lines, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the Union Steamships.
I now look at the eastern coast and I say- and I would be corrected if I am wrong- that every single coastal steamship line of the maritime provinces, and certainly of the St. Lawrence river, is paid a subsidy. These lines on the St, Lawrence river will be operating only part of the year, and they also have rail and road communication; the wafer is not their only means of access.
This raises one other point of great interest. The reason we have such a high freight rate is not only the mountain differential, but also the lack of road and bus competition which you have in the east. The result is that we have to pay the full traffic. Before we start with the 21 per cent increase, or the 25 per cent mountain differential, the people of British Columbia have good cause to resent subsidies for coastal traffic along the St. Lawrence river which results in cheaper sea routes and cheaper transportation along the St. Lawrence, which in turn must result in lower railway fares.
So apparently we are in the business of subsidizing coastal traffic in the east, despite the fact that rail traffic rates are lower, with the result, of course, that the prairies and British Columbia take up the slack.
I would ask the minister the reason for this amazing difference between $79,000 for British Columbia and $1,160,000 for the east coast, when most of these points are already serviced with either rail or road. You may have this new line servicing these little points making an application for a subsidy along the scale of that permitted in the St. Lawrence and Nova Scotia. If so, will they be given, shall I say, careful consideration, or favourable consideration?

To answer the first
question, one of the reasons is that the operators on the west coast are perhaps more capable of supporting themselves. Another reason is that there is a substantial amount for west coast services in the supplementary estimates. I am not in a position to say what

Then there is no chance of a section of the country which is now receiving inadequate service receiving better service?
I would not say "no" to that.
That is what it amounts to. If the present company is not willing to provide better service than the present inadequate sendee some other company would have to step in.
It is part of the contract that is entered into that adequate service will be provided for the subsidy that is given.
The contract was made forty years ago.
It would be reviewed every year. Any other company could make application.
Is it not true that during the war we had a Commodities Stabilization Corporation which handled some of these subsidies?
I think what the hon. gentleman has in mind is the stabilization fund that was operated by the Department of Finance. That was done away with on January 1 of this year.
Has that made necessary increased subsidies?
That is responsible for the increased subsidies which will be included in the supplementary estimates.
Did I understand the minister to say that they would not pay a subsidy to competitors on the same run?
That is right.
Would that mean that if a second steamship starts in operation the subsidy would be removed because, if there is competition, there is no need for a subsidy?
The first remains until the year is out, when it can be reviewed. The competitor may make application if he is operating at a loss. If he is operating at a profit he is not entitled to a subsidy.

I would think the new man entering a field would be more likely to be operating at a loss than the chap who
has the subsidy. Would not it be better to provide a subsidy for the two?
I am informed that that would be impossible to do.

I should like to add my support to the hon. member for Cumberland in connection with the ferry service across Minas basin. For some years the S.S. Kipawo plied across this basin, but when the war came along it was taken away for war service. That was perfectly all right but the people there naturally thought that after the war the Kipawo would come back and the service would be restored. However, when the war was finished the Kipawo was sold and has never been brought back.
I would point out that it is some 200 miles around this bay, which is a long piece for a motorist to drive when he is in a hurry or for a truck driver to drive when he is moving freight back and forth between points on each side of the bay. I think it is only fair to the people in that part of the country that that service should be restored. I understand that the subsidy was not large, and it would be a great help in having produce moved back and forth. It would also aid tourists and motorists who wanted to get around the 200 miles in a short time.
It would not be necessary to build wharves or anything else at Parrsboro, Wolfville or Hantsport, as these places already have good docking facilities. I suggest they should call at Hantsport as well as Kingsport, as Hantsport is on the main highway and more convenient for motor traffic. I would ask the minister to give consideration to having this service on the Minas basin restored.
in order to give improved service, is there any possibility of a subsidy being considered if an application is made?
The answer is yes.

Do I understand the minister to say that one of the conditions of granting a subsidy or subvention is that efficient service is being rendered? There are isolated points along the south and west coasts of Vancouver island where the mail is delivered by steamer only once in ten days. The steamer leaves Victoria, goes up the west coast, turns around and comes back, the round trip taking about ten days. Under modern conditions, to receive mail only once every ten days cannot be considered as efficient service. When passengers have no opportunity to go out to do their shopping or their business in Victoria more often than once in ten days it is not efficient service.
Surely if the subsidy were increased a more efficient service could be rendered. I know the Canadian Pacific is a large company and there are only small people who live out in these villages. I wonder if this large company is not trying to cover up its losses by charging high rates for freight and passenger service in an effort to make lip the lack of assistance that it receives?

I do not think I was using the word "efficient" in the sense that ray hon. friend understood it, or if I was, that was not my intention. I am informed that one of the conditions of granting a subsidy is that the service is essential for the economic needs of the community. It need not necessarily be an efficient service as my hon. friend understands it. He has referred to a service once in six, seven or eight days, but it is not on that basis that a subsidy is granted. It is granted on the basis of the economic needs of the community.

It seems to me that I smell a badly decomposed rat. The minister says he has taken over from the Department of Finance the operation which was carried on during the war to keep fares down and to meet advanced costs.

I cannot allow my hon. friend to say that. I did not say any such thing. I said that during the war the Department of Finance operated a stabilization fund which went out of existence on January 1. Since then and because of that, applications have been made for increased subsidies. That is not what my hon. friend is saying.

The necessity for increased subsidies must be due to the

fact that the stabilization fund has been discontinued.
And higher costs.

During the war we endeavoured to keep fares down, and that was a worthy object, but because of that we are paying higher subsidies. We pay subsidies to some companies, while other companies do not get a subsidy. How is a company that is just starting in to compete with a company that is subsidized? Actually it is not just $79,000 but close to $400,000, because the minister brought in supplementaries amounting to approximately $350,000. This means that $400,000 went to these selected companies on the Pacific coast, Union Steamships, Canadian National Steamships-
Not Canadian National but Canadian Pacific, and Union Steamships.

Just two companies. But there are many smaller companies operating and providing a vastly improved service, which have to compete with these large companies which the taxpayers are subsidizing to the extent of $400,000. That is not fair to the smaller companies.

If there is any company which feels it needs assistance and can establish that it is operating at a loss it can make application and it will be considered, but if the company does not make application, my hon. friend would not suggest that we go out and give it a subsidy?
No; what I am saying is that you are subsidizing these two large companies to the extent of $400,000, which probably allows them to charge less than a proper fare.

They are not subsidized on that basis but on the basis of an operating loss, and we make sure, through a firm of auditors, that they are operating at a loss and need the subvention in order to make receipts balance with expenditures.

I would also ask the same question with respect to the Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland service, which runs from Charlottetown to Newfoundland, and also takes in Montreal and other ports. This Newfoundland service is of great benefit to the farmers of Prince Edward Island. We are the only-island province in the dominion, and for that reason are more interested in transportation than any other province. We find that this Prince Edward Island-Newfoundland service
is one of our greatest assets for the shipping of goods by our farmers. Who are the contractors on that service?
The Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia service, which is called the Wood Island-Cariboo service, has been built up within the last few years and is operated by Northumberland Ferries Limited. No one can dispute that it is giving an excellent service to Prince Edward Island. One of the few things in connection with this service which the contractors do not have to look after is the docks. The docks at Cariboo are fair, but the docks at Wood Island are far from adequate to take care of the shipping that is done there. Most of the freight originates at Wood Island. I would ask the minister to give that matter his careful and sympathetic consideration.
As I said, transportation is the most important thing to our island province. I do not see an item in these estimates, but I hope there will be one in the supplementaries for a subsidy to a new ferry which I understand will be established between West Point and Buctouche. That is one of the parts in the western end of our province which has been sadly neglected, and I hope that some consideration will be given to it.

The operators of the service between Pietou, Souris and the Magdalen islands are the Magdalen Island Transportation Services Limited. The operators of the service between Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are the Inter Island Steamship Company, and for the service between Wood Island and Cariboo, Northumberland Ferries Limited. Does the minister know offhand the number of millions of bushels of grain that was shipped from Fort Churchill last year to the old country?

There is a decrease in this appropriation. I should like to know the reason for that. Is consideration being given to the whole matter of using the Hudson Bay route for the export of wheat? As the minister knows, western farmers have made representations to the government asking that this port be used to the fullest extent, because it will mean that farmers will get from six to eight cents a bushel more for their wheat. Because of the knowledge gained by the government during the war regarding the use of that port, we are anxious that full advantage be taken of it. I suggest that in the future the government make plans to have grain shipped there, so that we can have a real test of the Hudson Bay port and find out whether it is feasible to use it for both export and import, for cargoes coming into and going from western Canada.

The hon. member asks why the decrease. It is because of the increased cost of operation. There was a difference of $25,000 between last year and this year. On the question of traffic moving, I have already dealt with that on two occasions, and my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealt with it the other day.
